utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Kerem Gulay, who is an interim from Turkey and a Fulbright scholar, who is joining us today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, sir. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable, please. Mr. Tieger, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I note I appear this morning with Mr. Amir Zec as well as Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Excuse me, Mr. Tieger. Before we start the direct examination, I had one issue I wanted like to raise with the Chamber, and relating to the witness's diary. And I think it's appropriate to do it in the presence of the witness, but if Mr. Tieger or the Chamber feels otherwise, I'll stop. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the 11th of January, we learned that the witness had maintained a diary while in Bosnia, and particularly while in the custody of the Bosnian Serb Army, and we had requested that from the Prosecution on the 11th of January. They replied to us that they had forwarded our request to Canada on the 13th of January, and asked us to directly make that request of the Canadian Government, which we did immediately. And I understand from Mr. Tieger that the diary has not been produced, the witness didn't bring the diary with him, and it's not in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. So I would ask the Chamber to inquire of the witness whether he's willing to make his diary available when he returns to Canada, and he can redact any personal entries that exist in the diary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you well know well, Mr. Robinson, it has been our policy to intervene in the last moment, as part of the Tribunal, and leave such matters in the hands of the parties' voluntary co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it is the last moment, because we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Having said that, can I inquire of the witness, what his position is about on this issue. Mr. Rechner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have the diary in my possession right now. I'm serving outside of Canada. The original copy does not exist. There may be a photocopy somewhere, but I don't know -- a photocopy exists, but I don't have one where I'm serving now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have a chance to go back to Canada and find that photocopy, are you minded to make a photocopy which would be available to the parties, as requested by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, provided I can redact the necessary portions, as Mr. Robinson mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation to make, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We appreciate that very much, and we'll ask the Witness and Victim Unit to follow up on that as he returns. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, although your name has already been mentioned, perhaps we can begin by simply asking you to state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It's Patrick Anthony Rechner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you are currently with the Canadian Armed Forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your rank, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we first call up 65 ter 90213.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, do you recognise this document as your amalgamated witness statement, which incorporates portions of your testimony or evidence given previously in connection with the matters before the Court?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you confirm that this document accurately reflects your declaration and that you would provide the same information to the Court if asked the same or similar questions here in court?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I tender 90213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2170.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, I want to ask you a few questions about your background, but particularly with respect to your previous work in former Yugoslavia. But first let me ask you to confirm, as I believe you did in the amalgamated witness statement, that you joined the Canadian Armed Forces at the age of 18, attended military college, and were commissioned as an infantry officer in 1985.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You served with the Canadian Battalion in Western Slavonia in former Yugoslavia between February and May 1993 in what was then called Sector West; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And subsequently you applied to be a United Nations Military Observer, an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thereafter served in Sector South, that is, from July of 1994 to December of 1994, and was subsequently posted to Pale from January to June 1995; is that correct or at least approximately correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Approximately correct. I actually arrived on the 31st of December in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, first of all, Major, may I ask you to explain to the Court, generally speaking, what the role of the United Nations Military Observers was in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In general, the role of the UNMO military observers was to work with the different sides in the conflict, and we lived right in the local communities. What distinguished us from the other peacekeeping forces was that we worked in small international teams of commissioned officers holding at least the rank of captain, and we were unarmed. The main duties were to help supervise the following of provisions in cease-fire agreements that the different parties agreed to, and where we were stationed and where we were working, that was all with the agreement of the parties in conflict. That is, in general terms, what the UN Military Observers did. As well, we got involved in doing assistance with delivery of humanitarian assistance as we were able to, but that was not our primary task.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, in connection with your work as a United Nations Military Observer or UNMO in Pale in 1995, first of all, did you work with a particular team?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was the United Nations Military Observer Liaison Office to the Bosnian Serb Government and the Military High Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did that liaison office have a particular designation or name by which it went?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Like all UN Military Observer teams, we normally referred to ourselves by our radio call sign. So in the case of our liaison team or liaison office, we were called "7 Lima."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And specifically, Major, what was the role or duties of the 7 Lima liaison team in Pale? What did your team do?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We had a very unique function, different from the other military observer teams, in that our work was primarily administrative and political. So we did not go out patrolling or checking violations of cease-fire agreements and that sort of thing. Our job was to facilitate communications between the United Nations and the Bosnian Serb military and political authorities, as well as then, by extension, facilitating communications with other parties in the conflict and the UN. And in that way, we could also act as intermediaries if the Bosnian Serb authorities wished to get some information passed or received from some of the other parties in conflict. Our work normally involved communicating by telephone, both land line, commercial, and satellite, as well as a special United Nations satellite system known as VSAT. We also used a communication system called CapSat, which is similar to e-mail, and also fax machines, and those were means available to us to contact the UN headquarters, that is, Mr. Akashi's office, and the commander of the UN peacekeeping forces in Zagreb, as well as Bosnian-Herzegovina Command in Sarajevo, and on the Bosnian Serb side, the government in Pale, and also the Military High Command in Han Pijesak, which is located about 60 kilometres away. That's the Bosnian Serb Military High Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, you mentioned earlier that as a general matter, United Nations Military Observers were also involved in assisting with or delivery of humanitarian assistance. Did your team in Pale become involved with this kind of work as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. On behalf of the representative of UN Civil Affairs in Sarajevo, which at the time was Mr. Aguilar, we were involved in some meetings with the Bosnian Serb Government. That was primarily the Vice-President's Office, Professor Koljevic, and also the health minister, Mr. Kalinic, as well as the director of the Medical Services on the Bosnian Serb side, which was Dr. Sosic. And that was in our official capacity. Unofficially, we tried to ease the suffering in the local community. And primarily through Dr. Sosic, who also was the head of the hospital in Pale, we would receive some requests if we could try to obtain a small amount of some vital medicine to try and deal with a critical situation with some of the patients in the hospital. So in support of that, we would take it on ourselves to personally go into Sarajevo to try to get this from the UN medical facilities there. And, as well, some of the other military observers got involved in a more personal capacity helping, actually, individuals in Pale and the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, how large was the 7 Lima team?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We were -- we were a total of four officers. There was myself, there was Ole Zidlik from the Czech Republic, Thelmo Reis from Portugal, and Pavel Teterevsky from Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was there a team leader or chief liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yeah. At the time, it was myself. Since late April, I became the team leader and the chief liaison officer of 7 Lima.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did the team members live and work?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We lived and worked by renting a portion of a house from a local family. It was a three-storey building in Pale. Our office was a converted garage on the main floor, and our living quarters were on the third floor. And it was a three-storey house, so our living area was on the top floor. And the house was also inhabited by a local family with which we had regular and very cordial contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was that building located in reference, for example, to any official Bosnian Serb government or military structures?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It was located about 300 metres from what we knew as the Bosnian Serb Presidency. It was a complex of a hotel called the Panorama Hotel and a building adjacent to it that was used as an office building. So we were about 300 metres in a straight line from that complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago you mentioned some of the officials -- the Bosnian Serb officials with whom you had contact in the course of your duties. Can you tell us, please, who your main contacts were on the Bosnian Serb side, as a general matter, in order to fulfill your daily functions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: On the military side, the primary contact were two Bosnian Serb Army liaison officers who were based at the main headquarters in Han Pijesak. There was, first of all, Colonel Milos Djurdjic and Major Kralj. On the civilian side, it was primarily Professor Nikola Koljevic, the vice-president of the Republika Srpska, and also he was the chairman of their Committee for Co-operation with UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you deal, on a daily or weekly basis - you can tell us the frequency - directly with Professor Koljevic or with a member of his staff?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We did not deal directly with Professor Koljevic frequently. It was normally with his secretary, Ceca. Her last name was Savic. And that was very frequent, essentially on a daily basis. And the same with the two Bosnian Serb Army liaison officers; we dealt with them on a daily basis. And I should also add that we also dealt with Mr. Karadzic's office, that is, the Presidency, through his secretary, Mira, also on quite a frequent basis to transfer any correspondence or if we needed to request permission at that level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for clarification: You were a captain in rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to Mira, did you deal with anyone else in Mr. Karadzic's office or anyone else associated with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. I also had fairly frequent contact with Mr. Jovan Zametica, who I understood to be Mr. Karadzic's senior political adviser and spokesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, I'd like to turn your attention and our attention to a specific time-period during the course of your work in Pale, and that's to late May 1995, and specifically to May 25th, 1995. On that date, Major, did you become aware of an air-strike by NATO, or explosions generally, occurring in the vicinity of Pale?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. We had actually seen two large explosions occur at about 4.00 in the afternoon to the south of where we were located in Pale, that is, south of our office, a distance of something like 5 to 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At that time, did you know what those explosions were or were you able to go out and check to see what had happened?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, we did not know exactly what they were, and we could not go out to that area because we were under restrictions of movement at the time and we were not permitted to leave the Pale area. However, we did suspect that they could be air-strikes, because we had transmitted earlier a letter to General Mladic - that's the commander of the Bosnian Serb Army - from General Smith, who was the commander of the UN peacekeeping forces in Bosnia, threatening that if certain conditions were not met by the Bosnian Serb side and, actually, all parties to the conflict, that they would be subject to air-strikes. And in the case of the Bosnian Serbs, the first condition was that they had to return four heavy weapons back to a weapons collection point from which they had been removed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning your attention next to the next morning, May 26th, did you become aware at that time of further explosions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. At approximately 10.00 in the morning, a similar type of explosions like the air-strikes the previous day occurred. I should just, for the clarification of the Court, mention that after the air-strikes had occurred, approximately 30 minutes later we were informed by our headquarters on the 25th of May that those two explosions had, in fact, been air-strikes carried out by NATO on behalf of the United Nations. So then on the 26th of May, there were similar explosions, but much more over the course of about an hour and a half or so. We estimated it was approximately 10.00 -- starting at 10.00 in the morning, approximately, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at some point after the explosions began, did you become aware of any activity at your accommodations or office?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. A few minutes later, there was a couple of shots fired and some yelling, some loud voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where were you when you first became aware of those shots and the loud voices?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I was upstairs on the third floor, in my accommodation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Major, what did you do after you became aware of this -- of these shots and the voices?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We were aware from the news broadcast the previous day, and also by the reactions of our neighbours, that people had been very angry about the air-strikes there, so we were concerned who it actually was. We had also requested the previous day, on the 25th of May, from Mira, Mr. Karadzic's secretary, if she could ensure that our house and office were being watched by their security people just to prevent any local people trying to attack us for -- out of revenge or feeling badly about the situation. So I wasn't sure what was going on, so I went slowly down the stairs quietly to investigate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you find out?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I -- our office had two entrances. There was a main entrance at the front of the house which was the entrance to what previously had been the garage, and then around the back there was a small door. So I went around to the back. The door had already been opened, so I was able to peer in and actually saw and heard what appeared to me to be three Bosnian Serb people. I saw at least one who was armed. So then I went to the kitchen, where we -- that's across the corridor from our office, to where we had a telephone, and there I made three telephone calls. The first one was to Mira, Mr. Karadzic's secretary, who I'd spoken to the previous evening, inquiring -- or mentioning to her that we had some armed people in our office who had already been shooting outside. And I asked her if she could send someone around to investigate the situation. She then asked me what time they had arrived, so I said, Well, a few minutes ago, which would have been approximately 10.30 that morning on the 26th of May. And then she told me, Oh, they were sent -- she also asked me, Are they soldiers? And I said I couldn't really tell. They weren't dressed properly as soldiers in a full uniform. So then she asked me about the time, and I said, 10.30, and said, Okay, then they were sent officially. And I asked her what that meant, and she didn't give me any further information. So the second telephone call I made was then to Mr. Jovan Zametica, whom I had mentioned earlier was Mr. Karadzic's senior political adviser and whom I got to know personally, and I asked -- and I explained the situation to him. And he said, yes, he had also heard that something was being organised to send some people to our office that morning. And I asked him to clarify and explain what that was supposed to mean, and he said, just simply, I suggest that you be as co-operative as possible. And then I was able to -- had also our housekeeper there that morning. So I was then going to call the chief of police in Pale to send some policemen around just to verify that everything was under control. And as I was about to call, our interpreter from the office who was on duty that morning, Snezana Golijanin, came out of the office, started waling up the stairs and calling for me in a loud voice, so I turned to her and asked what was going on. And she said, You are required in the office. So then I asked the housekeeper to call the chief of police and went into the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in the office, Major, who was there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: When I walked through the door, I saw one person armed with an AK-47. That's a Russian assault rifle, or it could have been made in Yugoslav -- the Yugoslav Army also used it, made by Zastava, their weapons company, with hand-grenades, and he had a military camouflage pants and T-shirt on. And the other individual was someone I had met earlier in Pale on at least two occasions, who was a Canadian of Serbian origin. His name was Nicholas Ribic, and he was wearing a full Bosnian Serb uniform with helmet and also armed with an AK-47 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were any of the other members of your team either in the office or in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. Both Ole Zidlik and Pavel Teterevsky were in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was happening or what happened when you entered the office?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Nicholas Ribic immediately turned to me and said, Sit down, Pat, in an angry voice, so I complied. Also, I remember Ole Zidlik then was on -- was operating our radio in communication with our UN Military Observer or UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo, with Nick Ribic being next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At some point, did you become involved with the contact or the attempt to contact headquarters, that is, UNMO headquarters, via the radio system?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. As the team leader then, I took over control of at least our team's involvement and told our headquarters that we had some armed men in our office. And then Nicholas Ribic, who spoke, of course, perfect English, as a Canadian, started making threats that he wanted the air-strikes called off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did he indicate what would or might happen if the air-strikes weren't called off?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It started first with simply demands that the air-strikes needed to be called off. Then he mentioned, If you value the lives of your UNMOs, you will call off the air-strikes. And then I should also add we then moved -- switched over to using our satellite phone because it would make the communications easier, because on the radio net, a lot of people were. And Mr. Ribic was not familiar with the UN protocols for how you speak on a radio and procedure, was it was getting a bit confusing with our headquarters. So then we switched to the satellite phone, and then Mr. Ribic continued making his threats. And he got more and more angry and his threats got more specific. So at this point, he was saying, If the bombing continues, we will start executing your UNMOs, meaning myself and the other two team members. I should say the fourth one that I had mentioned earlier -- sorry for the break in the flow -- Thelmo Reis from Portugal, he was not there. He was away on leave during that period out of the country, so it was just the three of us, myself, Ole and Pavel. So back to the situation in the office. The threats got more and more specific, and then to the point where for the next bomb that falls, I will -- or one UNMO will be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of this contact with UNMO headquarters, and following the issuance of -- or the demand that the bombings be halted, and the threat about what would happen if not, were you able to hear the response by headquarters to Ribic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Only on the radio. And what they told him was that he needed to understand that the United Nations Military Observers were not involved in the air-strikes in any way and they had no means of communications to get them called off, that this would have to go through other channels. So perhaps -- I'm not sure because it probably was discussed over the telephone, so I didn't -- we didn't have a speaker on the phone, so it was only what -- I heard was what Mr. Ribic was saying, because then at some point Mr. Ribic turned to me and said, Okay, get me in touch with General Smith. So then I presume our headquarters told him that it was General Smith's office, that is, the UN peacekeeping forces, that would be able to get the air-strikes called off more expeditiously. So then Mr. Ribic told me to get him in touch with General Smith's office, and I called General Smith's office using our satellite phone, which we called them frequently. And I spoke with General Smith's aide-de-camp and said that we had some armed people in our office who were making threats against our lives and they insisted on speaking to General Smith. And then Mr. Ribic took the hand-set and started making the same threats over the phone to General Smith's office, his aide-de-camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After these calls were completed, did other people arrive to the UNMO office?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. After Ribic finished his telephone conversation with General Smith's office, he told us that his commander would be arriving shortly. So in about 10 or 15 minutes, another group of Bosnian Serb soldiers arrived at our accommodation, and they were led by a fellow named Srdjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After Srdjan and the other VRS members arrived, what happened next? Did you stay at the accommodations or leave?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, we were told to get our vehicle. It was a white Toyota Land Cruiser with UN letters and also "UN Military Observers" written in front of it with the UN flag. That was our official vehicle. So we were told to get it, and then we were told to radio our headquarters that we were going to be taken down to the site of the targets of the air-strikes, which at that time were still continuing to be bombed. And that location I was told to transmit was Jahorinski Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: En route to -- first of all, who was told to get into the vehicle? So it was yourself and who else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It was myself and the other two military observers in my team, so Ole Zidlik and Pavel Teterevsky. So we were all sat in the back seat, and the vehicle was driven away by the Bosnian Serb soldiers. And we had additional seats in the back, that's the cargo compartment, and a couple of them sat there as well. And then we drove away in the direction of where the air-strikes were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And en route to Jahorinski Potok, were you and the other UNMOs secured in any way?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. We were all handcuffed to each other with two handcuffs. So my -- I was sitting on the -- on one side of the vehicle, so my right hand was handcuffed to the left hand of Ole Zidlik, and his right hand was handcuffed to the left hand of Pavel Teterevsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, what happened when you and Captain Zidlik and Captain Teterevsky and the soldiers arrived at Jahorinski Potok?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: At Jahorinski Potok, it was a large complex, what we thought was some sort of large logistics and ammunition storage depot. We had not been there before. But there was a main gate there, and it was locked, so we were stopped at the main gate as one or two of the Bosnian Serb soldiers then went to look for someone to open it. As we were standing or waiting there, still secured by the handcuffs to each other and inside the car, a fairly large group of local civilians had gathered near our vehicle. And one of them then broke away from the crowd and went to our vehicle, opened the door, and started punching and kicking me. I had, unfortunately, only one hand to defend myself, so I got a few good punches and kicks in the process. Fortunately, though, the guards - that's the other Serb soldiers - were able to react in time before anything serious happened to me and pulled him off. Then he went back, that's the individual that attacked me. He appeared to calm down, and then suddenly he pulled out a pistol, chambered a round and pointed it at the vehicle. Pavel Teterevsky, the Russian observer, was very quick-witted, and he immediately opened the door and pulled us out of the other side. So we had the vehicle between us and this armed individual. And then the guards also reacted fairly quickly and managed to take the pistol away from him and unloaded it. But to our surprise, once the man calmed down, they gave it back to him. But that was, from our point of view, a very close call. Just one other thing regarding that incident. Once this man had calmed down, he asked me to come forward, so -- or he came -- I believe the Serbs took off my handcuffs. So I went to him with the Serb soldiers just to make sure, I guess, I was protected a bit. And he grabbed me by the throat and said that he had lost 12 sheep in the air-strike, and he said that was his livelihood, and he was very upset. And he also said that one of his relatives that had gone out that morning, they didn't know where he was and were afraid that he had also been killed by the air-strike. And so then he ended saying that he -- for those reasons, he should be allowed to kill me and I shouldn't be surprised at his reaction. And I told him also that we had nothing to do with the air-strikes, but he was too emotional and angry at that point to sort of discuss that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Were you eventually -- was the -- was access or entry to the facility obtained, and were you taken inside at Jahorinski Potok?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: After about 15 minutes, the lock had been -- they couldn't find the key, so they broke the lock with a hammer, and we were then driven inside the compound a few hundred metres in front of a large warehouse. There -- because the air-strikes, I should say, were still going on and we were still waiting to get confirmation from our UNMO headquarters at that -- or when they would be called off, so, anyway, we stopped in front of the warehouse. They took us out of the car and just sort of changed the handcuffs. So we were still handcuffed to each other, but we were able to stand. And one of us had his arm through the window of the rear seat, so we were actually secured, through his arm, to the actual vehicle so we couldn't run away or do anything. So we waited there for the air-strikes to be called off. It was perhaps 20 or 30 minutes. And during that time, one of the Serb soldiers, who was a lieutenant-colonel that we later learned was apparently the head of the press information organisation within their units in Pale and who had a video camera, he showed us his revolver that he took from his holster and pointed to two notches that he had cut in the handle. And he explained those two notches were for two people that he had already killed with it, and that if the air-strikes would not kill us by the end of the day, then he would come over and personally execute us, and he would really enjoy getting three more notches onto his revolver handle, indicating, you know, the three notches for the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he -- did the lieutenant-colonel indicate that he intended to kill you, whatever happened, or that it was conditioned in some way on air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: He was not clear on that point. It could have meant either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you receive any word from UNMO headquarters, or any other source, about whether the air-strikes would be called off?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Eventually -- that is, as I mentioned, we were waiting there about 20 minutes, so after about those 20 minutes we did get a radio call from our UNMO headquarters, and I can refer to them at Kilo X-ray. It may be easier than just repeating "UNMO headquarters" all the time. So our UN military headquarters in Sarajevo Bosnia-Herzegovina Command, also known as Kilo X-ray, gave us a call and said that the air-strikes had now been called off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after receiving that information, what happened, Major? First of all, were there -- was there any other indication or any further indication of air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Not -- they were not going in constantly. It was only every five or ten minutes or so, there would be another -- or even maybe 15 or 20 minutes. There was not a regular interval, but they were at least five minutes apart. I recall also either myself or Nick Ribic, the Bosnian Serb soldier of Canadian origin, would also be on contact with our radio and also telling them where we were being taken. So at that point, I believe Ribic mentioned that we would be taken to the actual site of the air-strikes, that is, to the site of the ammunition bunkers further into the complex that were being bombed that morning. So they put us into the vehicle, and just as we were about to get going another air-strike went in, so that is after we had gotten the all clear or the confirmation that the aircraft had been called off. The Serbs continued to drive towards the bunkers, so it wasn't clear to any of us what the real situation was, if the air-strikes had, indeed, been called off or not. Fortunately, that was the last impact, so that was the last air-strike, but it went in after we got the all clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Major, please tell the Court what happened after you and Captain Zidlik and Captain Teterevsky were taken to the bunkers.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: So it was the same thing as before. We were handcuffed to each other, driven down. It was perhaps 1 to 2 kilometres from the warehouses where we had been waiting beforehand. We arrived in front of four bunkers that were approximately 50 metres away from each other. Two of them had been destroyed. I presume it was that morning, because the smell of the explosive, the cordite, was very strong in the air. And Nick Ribic then reported on the radio that we're now at the site of -- he said "warehouse," but he meant the bunkers, and he said, Any more bombing and they'll be the first to go. So then they took us out of the vehicles and handcuffed me and Pavel Teterevsky to two lightning rods in front of one of the bunkers that had not been hit yet, and they handcuffed Ole Zidlik to the door of the bunker that had not been hit, and that was -- we saw was full of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, after you and the other two members of your team were secured to these potential targets, did you see other members of other UNMO teams brought to the same area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. About an hour and a half later or so, we saw our vehicle then being driven back towards the bunkers from the same direction that we had been taken there earlier, and we recognised members of another UN Military Observer team that was also based in Pale, but this was the standard patrolling-type UN observer team that was known as Sierra Echo 1 by their radio call-sign. So we saw them packed in their vehicle. The vehicle was driven by Serb soldiers, and they passed our position where we had been handcuffed, and then they went down the road. And then sometime later, 15 to 30 minutes later, then we saw the vehicle drive back past us and back to the -- in the direction from which it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know where the -- do you know what happened with these other members of the UNMO team?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: At that specific moment, no. We just saw the vehicle go past us and then come back the other way. But I learned later on, after a few hours, that one of the military observers, a Polish officer by the name of Janusz Kalbarczyk, had been taken down to where the vehicle went past us and handcuffed there in front of another bunker. And then the other four members of the team remained in the vehicle, and then they were taken to what I think were the warehouses where we had stopped initially while waiting for the air-strikes to be called off. And then also two of them had been taken to a bridge in Pale for a short period of time. And then I understood they were also taken back to the warehouses inside the complex. And one other thing. Before the Sierra Echo 1 team was driven passed us, about half an hour before that two of the Serb soldiers who had taken us hostage, they took the Russian officer in my team, Pavel Teterevsky, away. So after -- so for the first hour, there was the three of us from my team, and then after about an hour there was just myself and Ole Zidlik handcuffed in front of the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After securing you and Captain Zidlik to those positions, and initially securing Captain Teterevsky, did the -- did the Bosnian Serb soldiers remain with you at all times?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, they had only stayed with us when -- initially when they handcuffed us to the -- in my case, the lightning rod, and Pavel's case as well, and Ole Zidlik to the bunker, the lieutenant-colonel who I mentioned showed us -- had a video camera and showed us the pistol. He filmed us in that position for a few minutes, and then -- but I think they were concerned, because the situation was not quite clear what was actually going on with the air-strike, so they didn't want to spend any time there, so they quickly left. Then about an hour later, two of them came back. They gave me a box then to sit on. They moved Ole Zidlik, who was handcuffed to the door of the bunker, to handcuff him to a grate over a vent in the bunker which was lower down, so that would allow Ole Zidlik to sit. And then at that time, they also took Pavel Teterevsky away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at some point later in the day, did any VRS soldiers come to check either on you and Captain Zidlik or on the UNMOs who were further up the road?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. Then shortly before, about 2.30 in the afternoon, two soldiers who we had not seen before went up the road to check on us. And both Ole Zidlik and I, we understood Serbo-Croatian, so we could understand what the soldiers were discussing among themselves, and they were debating whether they had time to check on the other UNMO - they didn't name him - who was further down the road, because at 2.30, another -- or the air-strikes were supposed to resume. And one of them mentioned that he was there the previous day and there was no way that he wanted to be anywhere near the area if there were going to be more air-strikes. So all they did was they just walked past us quickly, just went to a little -- there was a little bit of a hill, and just looked over the hill, and then went back very quickly away from the location where we were handcuffed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, how long did you and Captain Zidlik remain handcuffed to the lightning rod or to the bunker?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I was there between five and six hours, so roughly from 11.00 or after 11.00 sometime, or 12.00, until about 5.00 in the afternoon. And Ole Zidlik was there until about 9.00 in the evening, so about nine hours in his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the soldiers who came to check at about 2.30 and were concerned about being in the area because of the possible resumption of air-strikes. After that, did you see others come to the area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Fortunately, no air-strikes occurred at least in our location at 2.30. So about an hour later, that is, 3.30 in the afternoon, there were two groups of military officers, fairly senior from the ranks that we had observed - they had some full colonels in the groups - came by to inspect the area, but they appeared more interested in assessing the damage, rather than our situation, but they clearly saw us. And then they were followed, about 20 to 30 minutes later, by a group of civilians who I supposed were government officials because most of them were wearing suits, with jacket and tie. And in this group of civilians, one of the members was Mr. Jovan Zametica, who I had known and who was Mr. Karadzic's senior political adviser and spokesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Zametica saw you and Mr. Zidlik there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. Not only did he see us; he came over and talked to me. And I should mention we were all quite close together. When Pavel Teterevsky was there, he was about 10 metres to my right, and Ole Zidlik was just across the road, about 20 metres in front of me, so we were all fairly close. So the delegation, both the military and the civilians, walked right between us. And then Mr. Zametica came over to me, and I expressed to him my shock and surprise how we were treated, saying, you know -- because up to that point I had thought maybe there was some sort of mistake, that this was an out-of-control group that had taken us hostage. When I had called Mr. Karadzic's secretary and Mr. Jovan Zametica, they never clearly explained what was actually going to happen in our office. So when I saw Mr. Zametica, I asked him what was going on and how he could justify the treatment of us. I explained that I had been attacked and so on. And he said, Well, times have changed, simply. And then in a self-satisfied way, he added a comment to himself, I wonder what General Smith will do now? And then he walked up the road. One thing I should mention for the Court - I don't know if it was mentioned before - another thing that distinguished UN Military Observers from UN peacekeeping -- the normal blue-helmet soldiers, is that we are protected under International Law as UN experts on mission, so we are internationally-protected persons. We all were conscious of that, and so was Mr. Karadzic's government and people like Zametica. So we were really shocked with what was happening to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, you mentioned a moment ago that you remained handcuffed to the lightning rod at Jahorinski Potok until about 5.00. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Then we saw our vehicle again come from the same direction, that is, as before, from roughly where those warehouses were, driven by some Bosnian Serb soldiers. They went down the road and then came back, stopped, and came to me, and told me that they would be taking me away. I asked where, and they wouldn't say, and they put me in the back of the vehicle where Janusz Kalbarczyk was already handcuffed, and I was handcuffed there as well, and then we were driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where did the vehicle go with you and Mr. Kalbarczyk?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: We went through Pale, where they picked up some more soldiers, and then we drove up a road to a ski complex called Jahorino [phoen], which was also -- Jahorina is also a name of a mountain, a large mountain in the area. It's a road that I knew well, because in the ski resorts there was a hotel named the Hotel Bistrica where some of the Bosnian Serb officials stayed, and including Mr. Zametica, where I had once visited him, so I recognised the road. So we were going up the road, and then it stopped and pulled off on the side where there was a track. And then we were at that point followed by at least one other civilian vehicle with Bosnian Serb soldiers. Also, a civilian journalist named Snezan Lalovic and his cameraman, as well as the lieutenant-colonel -- that's the Serb lieutenant-colonel, who was the press officer, who was the other cameraman. The Bosnian Serb soldiers, without explaining anything, just then blindfolded both myself and Janusz Kalbarczyk. Most of the other people got into the vehicle, that is, packed into it, because we then went up a dirt track with their civilian vehicles. It was a Volkswagen Golf was one of them, I recall, was parked. So then blindfolded, we started going up a bumpy, very steep track, going up-hill for perhaps 45 minutes or so. Because of the nature of the road, it was slow going. Then we stopped and they took us out of the vehicle, took our blindfolds off. And I found myself in front of a large radar dome, together with the same people that I had mentioned before, so several Bosnian Serb soldiers, the two military and civilian cameramen, the reporter. And as we were taken out of the vehicle and the blindfolds were taken off, two of the soldiers took their weapons - that's the same AK-47 assault rifles - donned black masks or balaclavas, and then Snezan Lalovic turned to us and asked if we were afraid. I'm not sure what the point of his question was, so I said, No, trying to appear as calm as I could. And then they took Janusz Kalbarczyk, leaving me where I was next to their vehicle, and they took Janusz Kalbarczyk to the radar dome about a hundred metres or so in front of me. And there they handcuffed him to the radar dome, filmed him with the two armed soldiers there with the black masks, and conducted some sort of an interview with Janusz.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, you've just told us that in response to Lalovic's question about whether you were afraid once you had arrived at the radar dome and the blindfolds were removed, that you weren't, but let me ask you: When the vehicle stopped and you were blindfolded immediately before being taken to the radar dome, what did you understand or think would happen?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Well, understand, I can't say because there were a lot of different scenarios in my head, but one of the things I couldn't forget was the threats that had been made throughout the whole morning, starting in our office, then at the warehouses and along the way, that if there would be any bombing, that we would be executed. There was also the incident at 2.30 with the two soldiers who came by, arguing among themselves if they had time to check on the other guy because air-strikes were supposed to resume. So I didn't know if there had actually -- any more air-strikes had occurred or what the situation was, but throughout the day, of course, there was a concern in all of us, and we discussed this with the other UNMOs later on. We were really concerned that we could be executed any time not only that day but throughout our captivity. But at that particular moment on the afternoon of the 26th of May when we were taken up there to the radar dome, my grave concern was we were taken there to be executed. The other thing that caused me to be particularly worried about that scenario actually happening was because on the way, as we were driving up this dirt track, one of the soldiers in the car turned to another one and asked him why we were going there, and he said, That is up to Jahorina, and the other soldier turned to him and said, Well, that's because Mladic wanted us to film some UN people there. And that's why I said he didn't say filmed in what way. So perhaps one of the things -- or I shouldn't say "perhaps." I mean, it was very clear in my mind. One of the possibilities was that we were going to be taken there to be executed, and probably filmed in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, you told us that Captain Kalbarczyk was taken by the men with the guns and the balaclavas to be interviewed. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Well, after that interview, which was conducted by this reporter also, Snezan Lalovic - he was with him and his civilian cameraman - then we were again blindfolded, put into the back of the vehicle still handcuffed as before, with all the soldiers piled into it, and then we continued -- and then we went back the same way down the dirt track. And then once we hit the main road where we had initially stopped and had been first blindfolded, then the blindfolds were taken off again, and we were driven to the Bistrica Hotel in the Jahorinski ski complex. And it was -- the word I'm searching for is "awkward" or extremely bizarre situation, because all of a sudden the mood changed to -- at least on the part of the Serb soldiers, to rather festive. They offered us if we wanted coffee or drinks, and they became very relaxed. I had been in the hotel a couple of times before, so some of the women who had been working there recognised me. So they came up to me, asked me how I was and everything. So it was completely as if nothing had happened at all. We then -- they took us for supper in the hotel restaurant, which was actually quite a nice meal. And so it was a very strange, for me, situation where sort of up to that point I had been constantly under a threat, and then all of a sudden everybody relaxed and pretended nothing had happened at all to us. So after the supper, we then were told by the guards that we would be taken to our accommodations to pick up some blankets and sleeping bags and coats for ourselves and also the other team members, because we would be spending the night at the bunkers or other strategic targets overnight outside. So we went into our accommodations, picked up those items. And then as we were going back through Pale, we saw another UN vehicle with Serb soldiers there, and it was another UN Military Observer team that we knew as Sierra Sierra 1 from a location called Kasindol. And I remember seeing a Czech, Pakistani and Dutch officer from that team in the vehicle. They were dressed in civilian clothing, which surprised us. But we didn't have an opportunity to talk to them because we were in the back of the vehicle, and only the guards went out to chat with the other Serb soldiers that were with the other vehicle to discuss something. I don't know what it was. And then from there, we were taken to a military garrison that was known as the Koran Barracks. We were taken upstairs to the second or third floor of a dormitory-type building. And there, for the first time that day, I saw all the other UNMOs. So it was a very relieving situation to see that everybody was okay. And the other UNMOs -- so there was, from my team, just Ole Zidlik, and from the other team, that's the Sierra Echo 1 team, there was Griffiths Evans from Ghana, Pepe Romero from Spain, Janusz Kalbarczyk from Poland, and Zlato Kukuznik [phoen] from the Czech Republic. They also had a Russian officer Dmitri Batiouchenkov, who was not there, and the Russian officer from my team, Pavel Teterevsky, he also wasn't there. And then there was also two members from another team called Sierra Golf 1 from Grbavica, which is a neighbourhood in Sarajevo on the Serb side, and there was two of them, Harley Alves from Brazil and Josh Gelasen [phoen] from the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Now, the next morning, did you remain at the garrison or were you taken from there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The next morning, the first thing that happened, and it was around 9.00 in the morning, Mr. Ribic and one of the other soldiers told me to go with them, and they took me outside of this dormitory building to our UNMO vehicle which was parked outside. And they told me to send a message to Kilo X-ray. That's our UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo. And they gave me a list of locations where I was supposed to tell them how many military observers were at each one, and it was basically the places where we had been handcuffed the previous day, so it was places like the bunkers at Jahorinski Potok, some warehouses. I remember a bridge and perhaps some other locations. So I transmitted that information and also took the opportunity to add that if Mr. -- next time -- or when Mr. Akashi comes for a meeting with the Bosnian Serbs, to please insist on having us -- UNMO chief liaison officer with him as a way of us to, sort of, not to be forgotten, and for the UN to try to involve us as quickly as possible in their dealings to resolve the crisis or whatever had actually been going on at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, let me ask you to take a quick look at a document. And if I could ask that 65 ter 10597 be called up, please. This is a code cable dated 27 May 1995 from Janvier to Annan. And if I could ask that we turn to paragraph 5 of that document. That's on the second page of the English. That indicates that: "The UNMO team from Pale, taken hostage during the course of yesterday, have been allowed to make radio contact with UNMO HQ in Sarajevo this morning. They report that they are unharmed, and were able to brief on the location of some of the other teams." Major, does that appear to be a reference to the contact that you had on the morning of May 27th, to which you just referred?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely certain, but it would appear so. It just mentions an UNMO team from Pale, so it could be us or Sierra Echo 1. But I sort of fit the description of the messages being sort of from a team in Pale that made radio contact and reported some locations of the other teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Mr. President, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, after making the call, where were you taken and by whom?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Then all of us that had spent the night together, so I mentioned the three teams, a total of eight UNMOs, we were then taken back to the complex that had been bombed the previous day. I remember, in the message that I relayed, that I passed on, that we would be taken back in front of the bunkers. And to my great relief, they actually took us not to the bunkers, themselves, but a few hundred metres before that, where there was a small guard hut. So that's where we were kept for the duration of that day. Although things were fairly calm, we saw in the back room they had about 10 sets of handcuffs laid out, so we knew that they were simply waiting for an order and we would be taken and find ourselves in exactly the same situation as the previous day. So we spent the day there. Also, sometime later that morning or early afternoon, the two Russians joined us, so Pavel Teterevsky from my team and Dmitri Batiouchenkov from the Sierra Echo 1 team. We spent the day there uneventfully. Later in the afternoon, myself and a member of the Sierra Echo 1 team, we were told to go to our accommodations, that we could bring back some toiletries and change of clothes for ourselves and the other team members. So we were taken there by some of the guards. And in the Sierra Echo 1 office, a couple of their interpreters were there, watching television, and they had satellite TV so they were watching CNN. And the interpreters told them that they saw the UNMOs used as human shields broadcast around the world from the previous day, and that also on the local Serb news in Pale, they had shown me, myself, and Ole Zidlik and Pavel Teterevsky handcuffed to those lightning rods and the ammunition bunker, and that the Serbs in the news broadcast accused us of actually being the people on the ground guiding in the air-strikes, which was not only false, but it infuriated us, because accusations like that put our lives in danger, because the local people had very little access to independent media, and we were concerned that now, especially given those who were angry at the air-strikes, they would then believe these reports and then seek to take their anger or frustrations out on us and retaliate against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Major, as your statement indicates, you were eventually released on the 18th of June, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That's when we left Pale, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some of the events or some of what you did during the period of time before that release. First of all, you indicated that you had been back to your accommodations. Did you go to your accommodations more than once between the time you were -- that you began to be held at the garrison and the time you were released?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, several more times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At any -- at some point during one of those visits, did you attempt to get someone to send a message to your HQ?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, that is now the 28th of May, so after the day we spent at the guard huts near the bunkers, I was allowed again, both myself and a member from the other team, to go to each of our respective accommodations to pick up some more personal items for us, because at that time it became clear that we would be held in captivity for several more days. And one of our interpreters was on duty, and I saw that since over the last three previous days, when we were no longer in the office, the UN confidential situation reports kept being sent to our office, so I instructed my interpreter to send a fax to our headquarters, to Kilo X-ray, and tell them to stop sending the sitreps, and also to report that myself and the other military observers that I was with, so from my team, Sierra Echo 1 and Sierra Golf 1, were being held at the Koran Barracks, and we were in good condition. And our landlord was there in the office. He did not speak English, as I was relaying the instructions in English to our interpreters, but he understood facts and something, and he intervened very angrily and said, No, no, no faxes, no telephone calls. Mr. Krajisnik had called, and he said none of this is permitted. Just do as you're told and you'll be all released in three or four days. And by Mr. Krajisnik -- our landlord, they were close associates in business before the war and were close -- I presume still close friends or colleagues, our landlord meant Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, who was the -- we understood at the time, the head of the Serb Parliamentary Assembly in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, during the period of time you were held, did you attempt to contact Professor Koljevic, with whom you'd had previous dealings, at least through his office?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I had another opportunity the following day, on the 29th of May, to go over to our accommodation, because we didn't have any facilities where we were being held to do laundry and so on. So we discussed that with our guards, and I suggested that we get our laundry done, as required, from our housekeeper where we were living, because we had already paid for the next month's rent, which included services like doing laundry and so on. So I went there to drop off some laundry. But before then, we stopped first at the Sierra Echo 1 team location, where one of my interpreters was on duty -- sorry, not on duty, she was just visiting there. And I told her that we would be leaving in a few minutes for my office and that I needed to get a meeting done -- organised with Professor Koljevic, because I still thought at this point perhaps he could intervene in helping us in some way, because I had some personal dealings with him previously in my capacity as the chief liaison officer. So I asked our interpreter to call Professor Koljevic's secretary, Ceca, and to tell her to call my office, that I had some urgent things to discuss with her. And probably that's all I said. So my interpreter complied, so it worked like clockwork. Five minutes later, when I answered the door to my office, the phone rang. My interpreter, who was on duty, picked up the phone, and turned to me and said, It's Ceca, and she wants to talk to you. So the Serb guard who was with us, that's was a fellow named Captain Vojvodic, who would be the main guard for the rest of our captivity, he was a bit surprised. But because the call came from someone from such a position of authority, he had no objection. So I spoke with Ceca, and I told her that I needed to get -- to meet with Professor Koljevic to try to find out what's going on, and also to discuss our conditions, which were unacceptable, and if there is -- and also I wanted to straighten out what the circumstances were about the air-strikes and so on. And Ceca then said, yes, no problem, she would arrange the meeting, and mentioned that it should be no problem at all. And then she asked me to pass the telephone to Captain Vojvodic, and I understood that she had instructed him that, Tomorrow a meeting would be organised with Professor Koljevic, and that this was all sanctioned -- you know, is all official. So when we left, Captain Vojvodic and I discussed it briefly, and from that discussion I understood that he had been told that, yes, the meeting would occur. Then later on, once we got back to our -- to the Koran Barracks, where we were being held, he asked me if Colonel Djurdjic, the main Bosnian Serb Army liaison officer that we had been dealing with, and the most senior one, could attend the meeting. So I said it was up to Professor Koljevic, but that I personally had no objections. So then he asked me to draft a letter, what we would be discussing. So I drafted a short letter that evening, saying basically what I've just said, that it would be discussing the conditions of our service -- of our detention, the circumstances of the hostage-taking, to explain everything to Professor Koljevic, how we had actually been mistreated and what had actually happened, and then to discuss the way ahead, how to get out of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the meeting the next day take place?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, it didn't. And I asked Captain Vojvodic, you know, several times during the day when it will be, and he said -- first he didn't know, and then he said he went to try to find out, and that there was nobody at all in Professor Koljevic's office and nobody else in the Presidency area that he could get any information from about the meeting. So he said nobody told him anything and he received no instructions about any meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you eventually meet with Professor Koljevic during the course of your captivity?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, eventually, much later on, the 15th of June. So that's, I believe, the 21st day of our captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm in the Court's hands. I can ask about that or we can take it up when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. May I introduce Kejia Guo from China and the Netherlands, who is joining us for this session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUO
utterances.text: Nice to meet you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, just before the recess I had asked you if you eventually were able to meet with Professor Koljevic during your captivity. And you indicated much later on -- that it did happen much later, on the 15th of June. And then again -- or that was the 21st day of your captivity, as you calculated it. Can you tell us about that meeting, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. It came as a bit of a surprise, but a pleasant surprise. It was on the morning of that day, Captain Vojvodic had come into our accommodations and told us -- or told me to get ready, that I finally have my meeting with Professor Koljevic, if I was happy, that he was able to arrange this meeting. I told him, Well, it's about time. So I was then taken with Captain Vojvodic. We drove to the military police headquarters in Pale, and there, in a room, I had a private one-on-one meeting with Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you relate to Professor Koljevic your concerns about your treatment and captivity and various specific issues you wanted to raise with him prior to that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, in great detail, and I was grateful Professor Koljevic had the time to discuss all of my concerns. The most pressing concern I had, and all of us up to that point, was that we were unable, except at just some very short and very limited periods of time, to make contact with our next of kin. By that time, all of us had managed to make a telephone call home, but for some of us, it was much later, such as the 10th of June was when I actually got to make a phone call home. And we wanted to not be limited to just one two-minute call once during our captivity, because, of course, our families had seen all the images that were broadcast of our use as human shields and were extremely concerned about our well-being. And that, of course, made us concerned about their well-being, how they were coping with the situation, because there was no information being provided to them by the Bosnian Serbs through the UN, what our conditions were. We were not able to have contact with the outside world. So that was the first concern. And Professor Koljevic responded positively, but he didn't commit to anything. He would just say he would see what he can do. Then we also discussed, in great detail, the actual hostage-taking and what had actually happened to us. I wanted to make sure Professor Koljevic understood everything. And he was a bit surprised. He knew about some of the details, but not everything, how we had actually been threatened and how the whole situation had impacted on all of us; not just my team, but all the other people. We then also moved on to discuss the working relationship between the UN and the Bosnian Serb authorities, and my team's role as the liaison office in that, specifically. And Professor Koljevic then explained that the air-strikes, for the Bosnian Serbs, had been accepted extremely badly. They were surprised at the intensity of them and that they actually had done some real damage. Up to that point, he mentioned air-strikes were really not much of a concern to the Bosnian Serbs. They had normally received prior warning, and they were typically symbolic, it was just one small, isolated target. But he said the air-strikes on the 26th, they were intensive, and they did not expect them to occur until after a 12.00 noon dead-line that day, which was for something else. It was a dead-line in General Smith's warning that all the shelling was to stop. But, anyway, he mentioned, for the Serbs, this was a big crisis, and they needed to react in a way that would send a shock to the UN. And he then used the analogy of an electric shock, saying that sometimes if you treat a patient -- a medical patient with an electric shock, you can kill him, but sometimes you can cure him. So they said from their point of view, this was all worth the risk. Then I asked him about our future relationship, if we would be released in Pale, but he said, no, the Serbs want to start a completely new relationship with the UN, so that our office would be closed. That's essentially what we discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned your access to your family, communications with your family, despite your requests. Were you able to -- did you request to meet with and were you able to meet with, for example, the Red Cross, the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Earlier on in our captivity, on, I believe, it was the third day or fourth day, I drafted a letter to Major Batinic, who was the superior of Captain Vojvodic - and, again, just to recall, Captain Vojvodic was the main guard during our captivity - because at that point we were already starting to get frustrated by the fact that we were not receiving telephone calls and other things. So we drafted a letter to Major Batinic, requesting telephone calls, contact with the International Committee of the Red Cross which had an office of delegates right in Pale that we personally knew very well, and we knew that was our right under International Law as well. We wanted access to medical care because some of the people in the group were under extremely severe stress. We wanted also regular access to our accommodations, and we wanted regular access to news. And the final issue that we requested was for me and my team to be able to work out of our office. If that was a concern to the Bosnian Serbs, they could have some guards with us, but we thought it would be important for us to maintain our role as the liaison team between the UN and the Bosnian Serb authorities and to start that up as soon as possible. So regarding the Red Cross, we eventually were able to meet them. I believe it was on the 8th of June, so well into our captivity. And I also found out from them -- they had also been insisting from the very first day, once it had been clear to them that we had been taken away, that they have access to us. That is, the Red Cross wanted to have immediate access as well to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned a meeting with Professor Koljevic during the course of your captivity. Did you also meet with someone you understood to be the president of the Republika Srpska Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. When the delegates of the ICRC came to see us on what I believe was -- I recall was the 8th of June, they were accompanied by Mr. Bulajic, who was president of the Bosnia -- or the Bosnian Serb Exchange Commission. This was the representative who would be involved in exchanges of prisoners between the Bosnian Serbs and the other parties to the conflict. And, in fact, I had met Mr. Bulajic once before as I was driving from Kiseljak, which was an area near Sarajevo held by the Croatian forces, and he had a problem at one of the check-points, and I was travelling back from a meeting there with a French team who was escorting him, and I managed -- because they didn't speak Serbo-Croatian, I intervened and managed to get him access through the Croatian check-point back into Republika Srpska. So, anyway, Mr. Bulajic came in with the ICRC team and introduced himself, and said that we were being treated properly as prisoners of war, since we had been combatants. And I took issue with that. I asked him was he aware that we were UN Military Observers, not other soldiers or peacekeeping forces. And he said, Yes. And I asked him was he aware that UN Military Observers are unarmed. He said, Yes. I said, Are you aware that we were working on the Bosnian Serb held territory with the permission of his president, Mr. Karadzic. And he said, Yes. So I asked, Well, then how can you consider us to be combatants? And he replied, Well, this is something we can discuss later on, and then just turned us over to the ICRC. And I never had a chance to have further discussions with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated earlier that you were released on the 18th of June, finally. Did you meet with Professor Koljevic again after that meeting of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. Also on the 18th, I had actually -- well, one was a short meeting by telephone. There was an incident where, as we were packing up our belongings prior to our release, we tried to take some of our office equipment with us as well, and that was prevented by our landlord and the Serb guards. And then Professor Koljevic found out about that and then called to apologise about the incident and to reassure me that he would take personal responsibility for the security of our office equipment. And then later that day, as we were taken to the military police headquarters, so again the same location where I had the meeting with him on the 15th, this time it was the entire group of UNMOs that were being held. We were taken there. And also I was met -- or I was -- I met there also with a group of 11 Canadian soldiers from our peacekeeping battalion that was stationed in Visoko, which is near Sarajevo. And Professor Koljevic then talked to both the Canadians, as a group, and then to the UNMOs, as a group, and he just mentioned that -- he apologised for the treatment that we had received, and that he understood a little bit because during his military service he had been imprisoned in a Yugoslav military jail as part of that time. And then he repeated the shock therapy analogy, asking us to understand that the Serbs were required to take extreme measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Earlier, when your landlord had intervened with something you were trying to do in the accommodations, you mentioned that he cited Mr. Krajisnik. In the instance you just described, for which Mr. Koljevic apologised, was that something that you understood to be done at the behest of the landlord or was there further mention of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: What had actually happened is I had gone to the accommodations first, and I'd taken my belongings and the hand-set to our satellite telephone, and Ole Zidlik, the Czech UNMO on my team, he went then afterwards, and he took the antenna for the satellite phone and the CapSat transceiver, which is a small blue box that's essentially like a hard drive on a computer that allows the system to be used over the satellite's network as an e-mail-type system. Of course, we were perfectly entitled to take this, this was our equipment, and I personally had signed for responsibility of that equipment when I had taken over as team leader. However, for some reason, the wife of our landlord, Mira Savic, had discussed that the antenna was missing, and she got extremely angry. She called Ole Zidlik an enemy of the Serb people, that he was trying to take this equipment, which was -- which surprised him very much because he was particularly close to her and the children. He did a lot of good every time he went on leave, he brought back lots and lots of sweets, which was something we all did, but he went really out of the way to look after the children of that family. So they searched his belongings but only found those two items, but not the hand-sets. Our interpreter was there, Svetlana Balovic [phoen]. And then when she saw the hand-set wasn't there, she said, Ah, then Patrick must have it. So then I was forced to come back to the accommodation to also return the hand-set, and then I had an argument with our landlord. And subsequently to that -- in fact, during that argument, he said he would report this to Mr. Krajisnik. And then when I got the phone call later on from Professor Koljevic apologising for the incident, Professor Koljevic mentioned in that phone call that he had found out everything from Mr. Krajisnik. So he was aware of -- so I imagine our landlord, Dani Savic, called Krajisnik, who called Koljevic, who called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I'd like to show you a couple of documents and then some video footage as well. If we could first call up 65 ter 18839. And if we could go to the third page -- it should be the third page in e-court, I believe. Thank you. Looking at that first paragraph, Major, it reflects, among other things, an entry by the VRS and into the 7 Lima house, and a threat to UNMO HQ that for every bomb, one of the UNMOs will be killed. It reflects that the threat was repeated to General Smith by phone, that UNMOs of the 7 Lima Pale liaison team were taken to Jahorinski Potok, the place where NATO conducted the air-strike. It further reflects requests by VRS soldier and then 7 Lima to confirm that the bombing stop, the gathering of a crowd, the team leader of 7 Lima beaten and threatened with a pistol; that UNMOs handcuffed to the car; and an answer from General Smith that the bombing stopped; a report by 7 Lima 9 that if air-strike continues, the UNMOs will die for the sake of NATO. Let me ask you, first of all, by way of clarification, 7 Lima 9, do you know what that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's my personal call sign. "9" means the head of the team or the commander of the team, so 7 Lima 9. Or over the radio, we say "niner." That was me. If I may also clarify. You mentioned VRS. The abbreviation for the Bosnian Serb Army that the UNMOs tended to use in their reporting was, in English, BSA, but it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what does that acronym stand for?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: "BSA," Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
