utterances.text: So that's the acronym for VRS --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Srpski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- in English?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So do these entries reflect some of what you experienced first-hand and are they references to some of what you told the Court during the course of your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn next to 65 ter 21963. And if we could go to the next page, please. And the next page after that. And just complete going through the two more pages. If we could show those, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, you've had a chance to look at this document previously, and can you tell us, based on your own experience and what you learned from others, what this document represents?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: This document represents what the UN headquarters in Sarajevo, that is, General Smith's headquarters, I believe, or it could be the Sector Sarajevo headquarters of General Gobillard, what they believed where the actual UN Military Observers who were taken hostage were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, I'd like to turn to some video footage, if we could, please. And I'm going to invite you, during the course of observing the footage, to assist us by indicating what is depicted there. In some instances, the footage may be moving slowly enough that you'll be able to speak over it. In other instances, we'll try to stop, identify the particular frame at which we stop, and you can speak about what's depicted at that point. If we could first call up P02024, please. And, Your Honour, in the 65 ter, the time code was 00:26:41 through 00:29:30. As the Court is aware, when these videos are placed in Sanction, the time code begins to run from zero, so the calculation will have to be made based on the Sanction designation, and then that will have to be, of course, to identify the specific portion of the video, added to the commencement time of the video in the longer footage, if necessary. I'll also attempt to assist by describing, to the extent possible, what's on screen at that moment. So if we could commence with 02024, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Reporter: Again the Serbs' ammunition dump at Pale was attacked by NATO jets, and this morning four bunkers were taken out. The Serbs reacted furiously, this time not with shelling but with hostage-taking. It was a time of humiliation for the United Nations --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Major, you are also invited to indicate when you feel the footage should be stopped so you can make a comment that pertains to your testimony? Can you tell us who is depicted here and where that is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is my colleague from the Sierra Echo 1 team, Janusz Kalbarczyk, and that's up at Mount Jahorina, the radar dome, where we were taken late on the 26th of May. That's the incident where I mentioned we had been blindfolded going up, and the soldiers, once we got up there, took their weapons and donned black masks. And Major Kalbarczyk was taken there and interviewed and filmed. And the previous footage that you saw, that was also what I recollect seeing on the morning of the 26th, the -- that is, the air-strikes. You saw the big plume of smoke and dust, that's also what we saw from Pale, from our accommodations which were on a piece of high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the record, this is shown at 00:26:58.4. If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "UNMO's military observers were held chained and padlocked by the Serbs to points of strategic importance, this Pole to an observatory and a Ghanaian to a bridge, telling his captors what they wanted --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if we can just go back. This is at 00:27:08.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise persons depicted here, and the location as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- on the left is Griffiths Evans from Ghana, and on his right -- or on my right, his left, is Pepe Romero from Spain, and these are both UNMOs from the Sierra Echo 1 team in Pale. And this is a bridge in Pale which I knew quite well. It was quite close to our accommodations, just about 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... captors what they wanted to hear." "Today, we, the UNMOs, saw that the NATO planes bombed a lot of civilian targets and a lot of civilians were killed. This is very bad, and it's a crime against humanity. We, the UNMOs, will appeal to NATO, especially Rupert Smith, to be aware that our lives are in danger." "Reporter: Three more UNMO officers were shown chained or --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop, please. This is 27:35.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise who is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is Pavel Teterevsky, who was the Russian officer in my 7 Lima team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... to steel posts in the arms depot that NATO had attacked. One was a Russian, another was a Canadian --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that's myself, and both of us were handcuffed to those lightning rods, the two of them that I had mentioned earlier in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... used as human shields, and accused, quite falsely, the UN said, of having called in the air-strikes. The third officer from the Czech Republic --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that's Ole Zidlik --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's at 27:51:5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- who's the Czech officer in the 7 Lima team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... the door of a bunker with ammunition still in it. Six other military observers are being held in similar circumstances. On the way to the arms depot and already in the captivity of the Bosnian Serbs, the hostages called their headquarters." "If the bombing stops, we will be set free. Otherwise, we will be killed. Over." "Just to confirm, what they are waiting from General Smith is confirmation that the bombing will stop? Over." "If the bombing starts again, I have been instructed to tell you that we will die for the sake of NATO. Over." "This is BSA soldier. Three UN observers are now at the site of the warehouse. Any more bombings, they'll be the first to go. Understood?" "Reporter: The UN was --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, we just heard four excerpts, broadcasted excerpts. Can you tell us who was speaking on those and approximately at what point those broadcasts were made, or those radio transmissions were made, or --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The first three were made by me, at the request, or demand, rather, of the Bosnian Serb soldiers that had taken us into captivity. I believe the first two were taken as we were waiting at the warehouses for the air-strikes to be called off, and the third one was as we were starting to go forward towards the bunkers. And the fourth transmission, where you see the text on the screen by the Bosnian Serb soldier, this is from Nicholas Ribic, who was the Canadian of Serb origin, who was the first person involved in our own hostage-taking. And when -- this was relayed, I believe, by warehouse. He actually meant the bunker, and this was when we had arrived at the site of the bunkers, just prior to being handcuffed to the lightning rod and, in the case of Mr. Ole Zidlik, the door of the bunker.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: "Right now, there's --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, I'd like to turn your attention next to 65 ter 40557A [Realtime transcript read in error "44557A"] through C. This is ERN V000-8393. The time codes are 0:38:16 through 0:43:02.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's stop first. This is at approximately nine or ten seconds into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this scene and who's depicted here, Major?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. This is our vehicle. This is the Toyota Land Cruiser I had mentioned earlier. And closest to the vehicle, looking left to right, you see my -- actually, let's go from right to left. It will be easier. Closest to the vehicle is Pavel Teterevsky, then Ole Zidlik, and then myself. Then the man with the crutch is Srdjan, who is the commander, or at least he was indicated to us by Ribic that he was the commander of the group of soldiers that had taken us hostage. And the location is the warehouse just inside the facility where we were waiting for the bombing to be called off, so still a kilometre or two away from the bunkers, itself, but inside that large logistics and ammunition storage facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the 65 ter number of this is 40557?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Did I misspeak on that? Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I didn't understand. Stay here with them." "Fuck it." "They should all be all --" "They should all be ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that's the same location, just from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you're referring to the image at 59.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So left to right, that's myself, then Ole, then Pavel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "He will die if they bomb, he will die for the good of NATO."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Major, you're obviously back in the vehicle now. Can you orient the Trial Chamber about where this scene is taking place?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. This is now we have left the warehouses where we had been waiting, which is the image that you saw just before this, and now we're back in the vehicle and being driven towards the actual bunkers and the lightning rods, where we will then be handcuffed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who was saying, "Tell them you will die if they bomb, you will die for the good of NATO"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That was Nicholas Ribic, who was the Canadian of Serbian origin, who was one of the Bosnian Serb soldiers that day who took us hostage, and he was sitting behind us on a bench seat in the cargo area of the Land Cruiser.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: "Kilo X-ray, this is 7 Lima 9. Over." "[Indiscernible]." "7 Lima 9, we've been instruct to advise you that --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're obviously moving on to a different scene. That portion of the video ended with, apparently, you saying -- that was you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Beginning a transmission that you'd been instructed to advise them. And did that transmission continue with some of the information we heard on the previous video excerpt with the radio broadcast?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. I -- as you may recall, Ribic was telling me to say that we will die for the good of NATO, and I changed that to that I've been instructed to say that we will die for the sake of NATO, to make it a bit more unintelligible and ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could stop for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've moved on to a different scene. Can you orient us now? And we're at 1:36.5.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. This is at the bunkers, so we've just arrived. You can see where the handcuffs are being taken off. And there I am with Nicholas Ribic, who is the fellow in the camouflage uniform and the green helmet, and behind him is Ole Zidlik. So they are essentially taking us out of the vehicle and to the lightning rods, in the case of Pavel and myself, and to the door of the bunker, in the case of Ole.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Wait here." "Oh, my dear Russian. Are you Russian?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who is dealing depicted here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: This is Pavel Teterevsky being handcuffed to the lightning rod by one of the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is at 1:47.3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Call, what's his name, Kozirev. He can save you. To hell with him." "Not the hands."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At 2:04.2, what do we see here, Major?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: You can see myself on the other side of the lightning rod and Ole Zidlik being taken away by Ribic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Find a wire, steel wire, something more flexible."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just what's being --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop, please. We're stopping at 2:31.9 for the major's comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you seen on the transcript below and the translation is there was three of us but they had only two sets of handcuffs. So they used one on Pavel Teterevsky, the second one on myself, and didn't have anything -- or didn't have a third set of handcuffs for Ole Zidlik. So they were looking for something, and then they made the decision to use Pavel's handcuffs on Ole, and then they found a piece of rope and tied Pavel, with rope, to the lightning rod.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's a reference to the portion of the transcript that indicates: "Find a wire, steel wire, something more flexible." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, and then they ended up finding a piece of rope.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There will be a lot of UNPROFOR members in this circle this evening, just to let you know."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And stop here at 2:53.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what's happening in this portion of the video?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yeah. In this clip, that appears to be our vehicle, and it's moving further down into that narrow valley where the bunkers were. So the person taking the photo is standing roughly where Pavel, Ole and I are now handcuffed and tied. And it's going further away from us, so further away from the original warehouses where we were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the other UNMOs who were brought after you and Captain Zidlik and Captain Teterevsky were secured there, and the soldiers who came to check on the UNMOs around 2.30 or so. Can you orient us, in relation to this portion of the video, where the other UNMOs and Kalbarczyk appeared to be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. So the direction in which that vehicle is travelling, that's towards where Janusz Kalbarczyk was held, in that direction. Just to clarify, we never actually saw where Janusz was held, because from our angle we couldn't see that far into the valley. So we just knew he was somewhere down there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At approximately 3:05.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is the bridge back in Pale, very near to our accommodations, where you earlier had seen Griffiths Evans from Ghana and Pepe Romero sitting down next to the railing with a UN flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And these comments were made at 3:15.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recognise anyone here at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The pictures are a bit fuzzy, but I see a man with a cane. He looks like Srdjan. Once, I think, you start rolling the video, it will become clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you recognise anyone else during the course of watching, let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So there's Ribic with the helmet. And on the right side of the screen, it looks like someone is putting handcuffs on him or doing something with him, is Pepe Romero from Spain. And in the blue uniform next to him, that's Griffiths Evans from Ghana, both from the Sierra Echo 1 team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's at 3:20.8.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Don't write this down. Memorise it." "Bomb civilian targets around Pale. Innocent civilians were injured and killed. This is an act --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So there you see Nicholas Ribic squatting - that's the man with the helmet - giving instructions to the two UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is at 3:40.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the man in the brown jacket, standing at the left of the image?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's Snezan Lalovic, who was the same reporter who then accompanied myself and Janusz Kalbarczyk later in the day up to the Jahorina radar site, and he's a Serb reporter from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've moved to a different scene. Do you recognise what this depicts?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. This is on the road to Jahorina, where, as I had just mentioned, Janusz and I had been taken. And we had stopped and were going to turn on to a dirt track. And I'm in the back on the left-hand side. Janusz, in the blue uniform, is on the right-hand side. And they are just about to put the blindfolds on us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is for documentation. It's not going anywhere." "What documentation?" "Let's see. Can he see through this?" "No. He doesn't even know where he is, he's so scared and traumatised. He doesn't know where he is."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And now we're driving -- that's the same road to Jahorina. And the flagpoles that you see on the left-hand side, in front of the vehicle, that's, I believe, the start of the ski resort portion of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we just stopped this at 4:28.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'd like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A, B, C all together or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Reid asked me to mention, and we've discussed it with the Registry, a portion of this exhibit is already in evidence. We've begun discussing the best way of clarifying that overlap or ensuring it doesn't result in any problems. No full determinations have been made yet, but I raise it and indicate to the Court that the resolution is underway. But I think for the moment, for identification purposes, it's probably best to admit this as an exhibit in its entirety, and then we can sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2174.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I might add, Your Honour, the same will be the situation for the fourth exhibit, the fourth video-clip we'll look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to 65 ter 40387A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the man in the suit with the gray hair, that's Professor Nikola Koljevic, the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's at 7.9 on the Sanction monitor and as shown on the numbers depicted on the video, itself, 10:52:10:12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So there's Professor Koljevic again. And the people in the military uniforms that he's talking to, they are from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia, not Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I understood that they were a special unit from their Ministry of the Interior. And this is just prior to our release on the 18th of June, and these soldiers or special police were there to provide an escort for us into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at this moment, the video stopped at 16.3 in Sanction and 10:52:18:21 on the time code shown on the video, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "I cannot make any official statement at this time. I'd like to say, on behalf of myself and all of my friends and colleagues with us, we're glad this crisis is now over. After 24 days, we are glad to be going back to our different units, and it's been a difficult time, but we are all okay and glad to be going." "How were you treated, sir?" "I'd rather not comment at this time." "Where are you going to be going to? Are you going home? Would you like to go home?" "No, I still have some time left in the mission. It's up to my headquarters to decide where they will send me." "Would you like to continue to work here in the Serbian side of Bosnia?" "Yes, of course, as well as any other side."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And perhaps it's unnecessary, Major, but if you could for the record identify the person who was just speaking.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that was myself. And the circumstances were we were all on board the buses, ready to leave Pale for Serbia. And there was a lot of newspaper reporters there, and they wanted an interview with us, and we didn't want -- we just wanted to get going. And Professor Koljevic came on the bus and asked or pleaded with us if someone would go, so the UNMOs asked me to make the -- that short statement, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if we could tender and admit this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, if we could turn to 65 ter 40202A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, Major, if you recognise what's depicted here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. On -- so you see one of the bunkers in the distance. That one, as I recall, had the -- was hit in the back of the bunker, which you can't actually see on the screen, on the left-hand side, and the back of -- a bomb went -- from the air-strike went into the back of that bunker and destroyed it. As you pan to the right, you see the lightning rod, and that's Pavel Teterevsky. And the red dirt that you see in front of him, that's the road from the warehouses in the back, which then continued to where Janusz Kalbarczyk had been held. And on the screen, it says the reporter is -- his name is Snezan Lalovic, and the cameraman is Slobodan Stancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... two NATO aircraft bomb Serb civilian targets in the vicinity of Pale for the second time. The Serb Army has been compelled to react like this as well. UNPROFOR members, that is, the soldiers who called for the NATO aircraft, are now in our hands, looking like this."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that's Pavel Teterevsky and now myself. And this, of course, is the first -- the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those comments were made at approximately 1:03.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Of course, nothing will happen to these soldiers as long as NATO strikes are not repeated."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's Ole Zidlik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At approximately 1:15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, if I can say something. You just heard a comment there about front-line. One concern we had, we heard what appeared to be like shots in the distance to us, further in the direction where Janusz Kalbarczyk had been later taken, and we were concerned if we were very close proximity to a conflict area between the Bosnian Serbs and the Muslims. But then the soldiers said -- told us, no, the front-line is far away, and that that was just ammunition exploding from one of the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There are also reasonable grounds to suspect that these soldiers were guiding NATO aircraft towards Serb civilian targets, but the investigation is still ongoing. This is just one of a dozen sites hit by destructive NATO bombs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if I just reiterate for the record that those accusations that we were involved in guiding those air-strikes or providing any sort of assistance whatsoever are absolutely false.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "All the others hit civilian targets, the places where refugees from Sarajevo were accommodated. "Following the NATO air-strike on Pale, members of the UNPROFOR --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: This is Snezan Lalovic, the reporter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... have been put under the temporary control of the Serb forces, and now we're going to ask them what they saw." "We, the UNMOs, saw that the NATO planes bombed a lot of civilian targets, and a lot of civilians were killed. This -- it's very bad, and it's a crime against humanity. We want to appeal to NATO, especially Rupert Smith, to [indiscernible] our lives are in danger. And we require that NATO ceases bombing of BSA and Serb targets or Serb territories so that our lives are spared." "Reporter: Have you any problems with the Serb soldiers?" "No at the moment. We don't have -- we didn't have any problem at the moment." "Reporter: You are from?" "I'm from Spain."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if I may just add some explanation there as well. Afterwards, Griffiths Evans and Pepe Romero, the two UNMOs you had just seen making that statement on the bridge. They told us about that, and that they'd been forced to make that statement with armed people threatening them. From what we observed, no civilian targets were hit, and there's no civilian houses near the areas that I observed; for example, the bunk ers where I had been handcuffed. Also, from our accommodations in Pale, we did not see any other targets hit, other than the area of this bunker complex. So that's all I can offer, as far as clarification, from what we observed about the targets that were actually hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Major, you indicated earlier in your testimony that you'd been told that the broadcast, the SRT broadcast, had accused you and the other UNMOs of being people involved in guiding the air-strike, and we see it in this broadcast. Did you ever, during the course of your captivity, have an opportunity to confront the journalist, Lalovic, about the allegations made?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to -- actually, very early on, on the late afternoon of the 27th of May. So that was the second day of our captivity. This is the day when we had been -- or we were told we would be taken to the bunkers, but actually only held at a guard hut a little ways away, where we had spent the day. During the course of that day, Janusz Kalbarczyk and Harley Alves from Brazil, they were taken to Mount Jahorina again to be filmed at the radar dome. So Snezan Lalovic came there to go up there with them and then came back with them, and stayed for a while. While they were gone, I went with one of the other UNMOs to our accommodations, and that -- I mentioned previously in my testimony that one of our interpreters at the Sierra Echo 1 location mentioned that we had been shown on TV and accused of guiding in the air-strikes. So when I got back to the guard hut near the bunkers, I mentioned that to the other UNMOs. And Ole Zidlik and I, we confronted Snezan Lalovic about these allegations, and he replied that -- well, we explained to him that it was absolutely false, and he agreed, but he said because the Muslim side and their propaganda, they lie, the Serbs also have to lie. That was his simple explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And here you see Ole Zidlik. He was moved from being handcuffed to the door to the grate in front of the vent to the ammunition bunker, just in front of me. So it's the same bunker. He was just moved so he could sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's at 3:09.3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They have been positioned at all crucial sites so that NATO could strike again, and we are going to visit some of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An objection, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second before that. This was merged with 40202B. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have it as -- I have it as slightly overlapping with P02153, and that was the nature of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that that was the bit already admitted as Exhibit P2153.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, what is your objection? Is your objection already moot, given that it is already admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, it's a remark. I hope that the Trial Chamber are going -- is going to disregard the way they have been called, these UN soldiers, hostages. I mean, the way these dialogues have been lined up --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is utterly -- first of all, it's not an objection, it's an inappropriate comment, and I don't think it should be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have another opportunity to make your submission or clarify with the witness, but it's not the time for you to intervene in such a way. Yes, Mr. Tieger, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, assuming that this exhibit -- yes, has been admitted, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we deal with the remaining associated exhibits. There are a couple of exhibits that have been already admitted, which is 11723 and 40511B. And except those that have been admitted during your examination-in-chief, the others will be admitted into evidence and given a number in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, it's not a major problem, but regarding the 65 ter 22011, which is a questionnaire regarding Mr. Rechner, the witness, do you have to tender it, given that it is a kind of statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With his amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, no, I understand that, Your Honour. I understood that that issue might be raised. It is one that might arguably -- it isn't quite as obvious as maybe some others are, but I'm -- given the nature of the amalgamated statement and its admission, it's -- if the Court considers that it falls close enough to being a prior statement that would have formed part -- that would have formed part of the amalgamated statement, I have no problem with that. In fact, Your Honour, I -- yeah, I accept the Court's guidance on that, which I think is it's -- so I don't want to cause the Court any problem. So it doesn't need to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. There's no opposition from the Defence in regards to the remaining documents, so thank you. Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Major. I would like to ask you whether you can confirm that while you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a UN observer, you collected information, and that this information was shared with UNPROFOR or, rather, made accessible to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: "Information" is an extremely broad word. What we would do, in accordance with our duties, is report the results of meetings. We would report to our headquarters if anything unusual occurred in carrying out our official duties. But if you think that we were going around trying to collect information on what was going on in Pale or about the Serb military, we were not doing any of that. As I mentioned earlier, our function was strictly as a liaison team. And regarding the other UNMO teams, as far as I'm aware, all the information that they would provide to the UN was part of their official duties only, which they were carrying out with the permission and knowledge of all authorities on all sides of the conflict. I should also add: The UNMOs, we worked very openly. When a lot of them would patrol, as far as I know, they always had a representative of the local faction for their won protection or security. In our offices, we had no encrypted equipment. Our radio communications were open. Almost anybody could listen in to them. So, no, we did not go around collecting information surreptitiously or trying to undermine the security, the legitimate security of any of the parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that you just acted as liaison officers, is that right, and that you only provided information on the content of meetings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Essentially, yes. If something unusual would happen during the course of the day, for example, we had a couple of incidents where we had our vehicles hijacked at gunpoint, once someone -- actually, a group of armed people came into our office and actually robbed the other members of my team when I wasn't there. These sorts of things we reported. We also went into Sarajevo, and on a regular basis, to drop off the original hard copies of correspondence that we had received for transmission, and would also pick up correspondence there to send to the Bosnian Serb military or civilian authorities; that is, your people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report about the feelings of the people, about the situation among the people, about what the situation was in Pale or, rather, places where you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Not as a matter of routine. I think you're referring to a report that I sent after the first day's bombing on the 25th of May, where I had spoken with Mr. Akashi's office. There's a fellow there that I knew quite well, John Almstrom, and I mentioned to him the concerns we had about the local situation; that is, that the people were very concerned, and in the media they had mentioned that civilian targets had been hit and so on. And Mr. Almstrom asked me then to send that information to him, but it's not something we did on a normal basis. I think you'll agree these were rather unusual circumstances, and I wanted to make sure that our senior leadership in the UN understood that these air-strikes were regarded as basically directed against the Bosnian Serb side, and because of the way that they were reported, as far as we knew, falsely, that civilian targets had been hit, we were concerned about our security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think that destroying defence capacities of the Bosnian Serbs does not reflect on civilians? You saw that things were destroyed that had nothing to do with collection points of weapons and so on, reserves of ammunition, et cetera. Did you understand that that had nothing to do with civilians and their feeling of safety and security?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I can't comment on what the civilians thought of military targets being bombed. And if you're also asking why those targets were bombed, and not collection points, I'm not in a position to know why those sorts of decisions were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of Mr. Almstrom?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: He was one of the senior advisers to Mr. Akashi, and I knew him well because he is a former Canadian military officer and happened to be my first commanding officer when I started serving as an infantry officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that Mr. Almstrom was not in the UNMO chain; rather, he was in UNPROFOR, and it was from that position that he asked you to report to him; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I should clarify. Our liaison office was not strictly only for UNMO business. We were the only UN liaison office in Pale. There was a small UN High Commissioner for Refugees, two UN people, but they had a different function. So we actually acted as a liaison office also for Mr. Akashi's office and other UN elements in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was not unusual for us to get letters or other requests sent to us directly from his office to transfer to your office, and vice versa. For example, if we received something from your office for him, we would send it directly to Mr. Akashi's office and just inform our headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the liaison function, as it were, but this is what I'm interested in: First of all, the information that you had and that you collected, was it accessible to UNPROFOR? And in addition to that, what you told us today, could UNPROFOR put a task before you, could they ask for something, and were you supposed to get it for them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Your question is too general. I don't know what you mean by "information" and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You described what "liaison" meant. There is no contest there. I would be interested in the following: Your reports, your UNMO reports, were they accessible to UNPROFOR? That is one question.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: By "UNPROFOR" -- or "UNMO reports," you mean the reports from my office only?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Inter alia, your office, but all of this went through UNMO channels. However, was it accessible to UNPROFOR, as such?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand where you're going. We had -- there was a separate chain of reporting that the UN Military Observers had through their own system. As I mentioned, we were a distinct organisation from the UNPROFOR peacekeeping forces, so that's where the reporting went. However, at each level within the UNPROFOR, there was normally a co-located UNMO office. So, for example, in General Smith's headquarters in Sarajevo, at UNPROFOR headquarters as it was known then, there was the UNMO office, UNMO headquarters, BH Command. At the Sarajevo UNPROFOR headquarters, there was located an UNMO Sector Sarajevo headquarters, and so on. So they would maintain contact and pass information back and forth as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, you shouldn't really be speculating as to what it is I'm getting at. I'm not speculating about anything, and I'm not trying to blame anyone. I'm just trying to establish the nature of your links. The second question is whether UNPROFOR could send requests to you, asking you to do something. Could they give you tasks, assignments, as Mr. Almstrom did this time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In this time, it wasn't a task; it was just a request. They could ask us -- send us requests, but they could not send us tasks; for example, order us to do things. It would have to be approved through the UNMO chain of command. So if it was something straightforward, a request, normally at each level the UNMOs acted upon it. If it was something more serious, more complicated, more difficult, then we would perhaps have to get it approved at a higher level in the UNMO organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was your understanding; right? It was your understanding that both warring parties in the zone of Sarajevo, the Serbs and the Muslims, violated, in different ways, the cease-fire agreements that had been reached, or the total exclusion zone, in respect of heavy weaponry; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I recall there were violations. But our office was not involved in investigating them and so forth, so I cannot provide more information regarding your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, you know that the Muslim side was never bombed; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Bombed by who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The United Nations, or, rather, NATO.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: By "bombing," do you mean air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, on page 11 of the transcript, you confirmed that NATO carried out air-strikes against Serb positions on behalf of the United Nations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That's the way it was reported in the press. I'm not sure how the link between the UN and NATO is in conducting the air-strikes, but I can confirm that the aircraft were NATO aircraft, not United Nations aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on page 11, you characterised it as NATO air-strikes on behalf of the United Nations. Do you agree that these NATO air-strikes were asked for by the UN commander in Bosnia? I don't know which line it is, but it is page 11. I think the line is 12 or 13.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Are you referring to my amalgamated witness statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, in the transcript of today's LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I read it for you. That part is: "Yes. At approximately 10.00 in the morning, a similar type of explosion like the air-strikes the previous day occurred. I should just, for the clarification of the Court, mention that after the air-strikes had occurred, approximately 30 minutes later we were informed by our headquarters, on the 25th of May, that those two explosions had, in fact, been air-strikes carried out by NATO, on behalf of the United Nations." That's the transcript of what you said, and Mr. Karadzic referred to that part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I would have known that based on the letter that I had received from General Smith to General Mladic, warning him to return those weapons into the weapons collection points unless there would be air-strikes. And it was just common knowledge that if air-strikes were required, there was a system in place where the UN would request NATO to carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know or do you agree that these NATO air-strikes were carried out two hours before the UNPROFOR dead-line expired, two hours before the ultimatum expired?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 26th or 25th of May? We were just talking about the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 25th, the beginning of the bombing that was preceded by an ultimatum. There were only two hours left. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I would have to look at the original letter. I don't have it in front of me, and I haven't seen it in the many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm that on the 25th of May, I was in Banja Luka? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, based on information from your secretary, because I had a request from Mr. Akashi's office to try to find you, that they had -- they needed to discuss something with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have a look at 65 ter 32390. It's an intercept. It's a conversation of mine with General Milovanovic about this ultimatum. I hope that we have a translation too. I'm not sure, but I'll read it out. It's the 25th of May, 1995, at 1530 hours. Ah, yes, here is the translation as well. Milovanovic says -- well, he is greeting Karadzic, and so on and so forth. That is not important. And then Karadzic says: [In English] "Akashi's been after me all day. I didn't want to talk to him. I just -- he managed to find me. He asked me if I could do something in the next few minutes. Is it that difficult to give back those four weapons, some four weapons? Nikola is here too, he is hearing it," and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please cast a glance at this. Do you see that I've been given a few minutes to achieve that from Banja Luka, to have these four weapons returned to the collection points?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Just bear with me. I will have a read through the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could all the participants please read all of this, because our position is contained there. There is also a reference to Western Slavonia, that had fallen a month before that, although it was a protected area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the time, it says "1543" on top, so that was if the air-strikes occurred at 1600. Again, in my recollection, that's approximate. But let's use 1600 as a reference. Then that would mean it's 17 minutes beforehand. However, when the actual dead-line was for those weapons to be returned, I'm not sure if it was 1600. I believe it was earlier. But as I mentioned before, I'd have to look at the original letter to see what the actual dead-line was. The letter, just for clarification, was sent to General Mladic the previous day. So he had more than 17 minutes to return them. And perhaps there were also discussions earlier on that subject, but that's -- I don't want to speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] "I told him I can't even get in touch in a few minutes, let alone do something about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that right? In our circumstances, when situations were difficult, it was difficult to achieve anything within a few minutes from Banja Luka by phone. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I can't comment on that. I don't know about your circumstances, and the communications means, and systems that you had available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, following our practice, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D987, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to display a document from the news agency France-Presse, 65 ter 10726.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You noticed, in the previous document, that our position was that if Serbs were bombed, the United Nations could no longer be considered as peacekeepers, but would be considered as enemies; right? We saw that in the previous document, if you remember. You've read it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: These are your words, as far as I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to look at this report from AFP relating what I said in a public statement on Radio Banja Luka on the 25th of May. We say the same thing; namely, that if we should be attacked, we would consider it as an attack, and in that case the United Nations would be, to us, an enemy, a warring party?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That's what you stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, Major, of the difference between close air support and air-strikes as a punitive measure that changes the situation on the ground, in other words, diminishes the combat capability of one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: There are -- an air-strike is simply dropping a bomb, so -- and "close air support" is also a fairly general term. So as I mentioned, I'm -- well, neither at that time, nor since then, have I been trained as a forward air controller, so I can't get into the subtleties of these differences, in terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. So we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could introduce Aiofe Nichearbhaill, from the National University of Galway, who is with us this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may remind you, Major, would you agree that close air support is meant for the self-defence of UNPROFOR units when they find themselves in difficulty?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I don't know how it was defined specifically for UNPROFOR. That is, I don't know how close air support was specifically defined for UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that General Mladic gave a free hand to UNPROFOR generals, in case they are attacked by our forces, that they were free to respond and that would have no consequence on our relationship?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that air-strikes are something entirely different, that it's not just self-defence on the part of the UNPROFOR; it's a strike against one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, I'm not aware of how you should distinguish those two terms, air-strikes and close air support.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see that document again, the one we had a moment ago on the screen, 65 ter 10726. It has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the content of this document consistent with what was said -- what I said; namely, that in the case of an attack by the UNPROFOR, by the UN, the UN would no longer be regarded as a peacekeeper, but as a warring party? If it was published on the 25th, that means it had been said on the 24th. Is it consistent with what you heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, two different questions posed. With respect to the first, in case it arises again, it cannot be an appropriate question to a witness, to present him with two documents he hasn't seen before and ask him if -- the extent to which they may be consistent. The last document seems to be -- to have something to do with the witness's knowledge and experience, and that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe the witness is able to answer whether it is consistent with the knowledge he had at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the consistency question, I recall that there was a press statement made by Mr. Karadzic around that time. I can't say whether it was the 24th, or the 25th, or earlier. And I do recall him saying something to the effect that -- as reported here, that use of air-strikes or bombing, perhaps close air support - I don't know the exact terms that were used - would lead Mr. Karadzic to consider the UN peacekeeping force as something perhaps like an enemy, but I can't say if those were the exact words or accurate. But it's something along those lines, but how general or how specific it was, I can't comment further, especially after so many years.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to refresh your memory, then, Major. I'll call 65 ter 12143 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting: Do you agree that the strikes began on the 25th of May, and on that day you were asked to stay in your accommodation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: My first awareness of those air-strikes occurring was those two bombs that we observed on the 25th of May, and we were also -- I wouldn't say "asked." We were ordered. It was made very clear. We were not permitted to leave our accommodation. And that was -- that order was sent to us by the Bosnian Serb Army Liaison Office, so either Colonel Djurdjic or Major Kralj. And we understood it, from our perspective, that we were being put under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the problem is probably in the interpretation. The word I used can be translated as both "asked" and "required." Could you take a look at this document. Is this something you sent to Mr. Almstrom? I don't see his rank, but is this the document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It appears to be, yes. And Mr. Almstrom was a civilian at that point. He was not a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention: [In English] "they repeated Karadzic's previous statements that if the UN would use air-strikes against the Serbs, the Serbs would no longer consider the UN troops as peacekeepers, but as enemies."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was waiting for the interpretation. Was that, indeed, the position we took at the time, and as we see from this report, that position was very well known to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: In this report, I'm -- in paragraph 1 and those five bullets, I'm just summarising what was reported on a news summary by the Serbian Radio Broadcasting Service in Pale on the local television. But if you're asking if this was, in fact, what I understood was being reported, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 3. It reflects your comments and conclusions; correct? I kindly ask all parties to read 3: [In English] "The bombing caused and continues to cause considerable alarm among Serb civilians both in Pale and among their relatives and friends throughout the former Yugoslavia. Immediately after the attack and before the news broadcasts began, friends and relatives of the family we lived with, as well as of our neighbours, began calling to determine what the --" [Interpretation] Next page, please: [In English] "... what the situation was ..." [Interpretation] Well, let me not read all of it. The parties can read for themselves, and then the next paragraph -- the whole text, in fact. In this paragraph, you note, quite correctly, that 60 to 70 per cent of the population of Pale were, in fact, refugees who had already fled from other areas, and they were even worse hit by all of this than the others: [In English] "The state of fear continues among the civilians. Just five minutes ago, the father of one of our interpreters called from Ilidza to check ..." And so on and so on: "One should bear in mind that well over half (60 to 70 per cent at least) of the population of Pale are refugees, themselves, and are very sensitive to anything that could be perceived as putting their lives in danger again." [Interpretation] This is your observation and your conclusion at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It was my observation, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask to see the last paragraph: [In English] "As far as the locals see it, the UN is (once again) singling out the Serbs for blame regarding the events of the last few days in Sarajevo. While they are aware of the official reasons for the air-strikes (the four guns), they cannot understand why the Muslims go unpunished for the shelling and shooting that they inflict on Serb civilians in and around Sarajevo. In the minds of the locals, the Muslims started the recent surge in fighting, and the Serbs get punished for defending themselves. Furthermore, the local press agency reports create an overall impression that NATO has gone so far as to completely disregard the safety of civilians in this latest attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That, again, was your observation and your conclusion; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: My observation was on the local perception, which is based on the news reports and other information that they received from the Bosnian Serb leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in your view, was it really true that civilians were panic-stricken and furious?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I can only comment on the ones that we had access to, which were the family that we were living with, our interpreter who was on duty at the time, and some of the neighbours around us, but I can't talk about the general perceptions or -- further around Sarajevo. I was unfortunately generalising a bit in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of an associated exhibit that had been already admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be assigned Exhibit P2177.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 65 ter 19300.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, Exhibit P2178, also part of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a debriefing memorandum from you, right, your report and the report of Major Westlund? Can we see the next page. We need to look for the passage which contains your qualification that civilians were panic-stricken and furious. It's the entry for the 25th and 26th of May. Perhaps it's on the previous page. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think on e-court, page number 8. If we could find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25 and 26 May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember this debriefing and this qualification, civilians terrified and furious?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes. Those were not my words, though. That was drafted by another individual who was debriefing me. But that was the -- it came out of our conversation, so it's accurate, again, as I just mentioned before, to the immediate surroundings in Pale where we were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at the entry for the 15th of June, page 2, paragraph 81 and 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You relate here your discussion with Professor Koljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. On the 26th of May -- I don't need to tender this. It's an exhibit. On the 26th of May, at the time when you were captured, were you in the active service of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "active service."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you serving then, were you on duty, were you in the service?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I was employed as a UN military observer. That means I was sent there by the Canadian Forces to work as a UN military observer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see again P2172 for a moment, speaking of your estimates. This document has been exhibited today. Page 3. Rather, page 2, the next page. 8166, that's the page: [In English] "... panic amongst civilian and military is assessed as high."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with what you observed, that it was a state of panic? Do you agree with this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I'm still looking for the passage that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first three lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, the first three lines. All I can say is panic among the civilians in the immediate vicinity where I was living, that is correct. As far as others or the military, I cannot assess. For example, the Bosnian Serb Army soldiers who came to take us hostage on that morning, they did not appear panicked at all, just angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those who drew guns and who lost their sheep and their families, did they look to you both terrified and furious, panic-stricken?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that question assumes facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You need to put that question. Please reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, you testified today in-chief that you had suffered an outburst of anger on the part of a man who later calmed down and complained that he had lost a number of sheep, over 10, I think, and he had lost a relative. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I remember that's what he told me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you qualify his state as fury, or panic, or both?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The word I would use -- it was translated as "fury" in English. I would rather say just "anger."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now ask you to look at the second paragraph of para 3: [In English] "In such conditions when life of UN personnel cannot be guaranteed, and when the possibility of directing involving the UNPROFOR in military activity against one of the warring factions (BSA), regular armed forces cannot be excluded, then it is strongly recommended not to continue air-strikes in such conditions." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this general assessment by the UNMO command?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I cannot comment on it, because I don't know what information he had at his disposal to make that assertion. I had very little information. All I knew was the air-strikes that had occurred in Pale. That, I could observe, and my own treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you don't dispute that this is an official report, or, rather, a general assessment made by the headquarters of the UNMOs at the Sarajevo UNPROFOR headquarters? That's written at the top.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: It's some sort of an assessment. But what its purpose is and where it's being sent, I don't know, but it appears to be an official report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to repeat the same question in relation to others. Were all the others who were taken prisoner together with you in the active service of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All the others who were captured together with you, from your observation post and the neighbouring observation post, were all of them in active service?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The people that I was held with, that's my teams here, Sierra Echo 1 and Sierra Golf 1, they were not observation posts, they were UNMO teams, and they were taken at their accommodations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Were they in active service at the time when they were taken prisoner, just like you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if the translation is correct, "active service." Do they mean on duty, as opposed to being on holidays, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you serving, were you on duty?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: The term we would use, you're on duty. I mean, people could be away on leave or they could be at their post. Instead of going away, they pass some of their leave days there. As far as I'm aware, everyone from my team -- well, I can say not -- I know definitely for my team, and I presume from the other two UNMO teams, they were all on duty, which means not on holidays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your captivity, were you ever told that you were treated as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Twice. Once on the evening of the 27th of May, by Captain Vojvodic, when we were upstairs in that dormitory building, in the room where we spent the night. When he introduced himself to us, he told us that we were prisoners of war of the Bosnian Serb Army. And the second -- actually, that was the only place it was actually used, the term "prisoners of war." Mr. Bulajic, when he called us combatants, I think, was going to say that we were prisoners of war, but he never mentioned that. He just talked about us being taken captive as combatants.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, here in this 65 ter 19300 that we looked at a moment ago, on page 5 - we don't have to recall that document - you say that you have been informed that you were POWs. Can we now see 65 ter 22011. It's the questionnaire you filled in immediately after release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, in fact, you confirmed that today, that Bulajic was the president of the Committee for the Exchange of POWs on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I don't know if it was specifically for POWs. I was told he was the president of what was called the Serb Exchange Commission, and I know they were involved in negotiating exchanges of prisoners. But as far as prisoners of war or what that status meant to you, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see your response to question number 20. I think it's the third page from here. 1037307 is the ERN number. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the question for us, as well as your answer, number 20? Could you read it out, please, just your answer.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Well, it says: "During the ICRC visit on 8th of June, 1995, Mr. Bulajic (president of the Bosnian Serb Exchange Commission) stated to us that we were POWs officially because we were combatants. I had a short argument with him." So perhaps he did use the word POWs or prisoners of war, but what got my attention was that he referred to us as combatants.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since this is part of the transcript now, we don't need to have the questionnaire admitted. Could we now have 1D3067.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: Major, you -- or I don't know whether you, personally, but you, as a group, asked for certain rights and certain privileges; among other things, for a visit from the Red Cross, from a doctor, and your right to receive information, or, rather, watch television; right? We have a translation of this document, too, so could we have both on the screen? Is that right, Major, that you put forth certain requests, certain demands to the Serb Army, the things that I referred to; a visit by the Red Cross, a visit by a doctor, and the right to watch television, or, rather, to receive information through the media?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, those things -- visit by the Red Cross, visit by a doctor, and right to receive information through the media, that is, newspapers or television, those were things that we were demanding, yes, and not because anyone called us prisoners of war, because we considered that to be completely unjust for us to have been taken captive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You asked for that in accordance with International Law, international norms. I think that you referred to that today as well. You asked for that in accordance with international norms. Have you heard of hostages being referred to in any way in international norms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Referred in any way? What international norms do you mean? The Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Any. For example, the International Law of War, is it envisaged that hostages can make certain requests or demands, and are they responded to or are they met? What do the hostages invoke when they say that they want this or that or the other thing? You referred to International Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the reality of the position is that is a question that would test most professors of International Law and give rise to an enormous debate and probably an enormous written opinion. With great respect to this officer, I don't think he would begin to claim to have that sort of expertise, so I think what you need to do is to address that question in another forae, rather than put it to this witness. I doubt very much -- I can't speak for him, and I don't, but I doubt very much whether he has an exhaustive knowledge of this topic that would be required to answer that question with the particularly that you require.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I mean, all I'm aware of is that taking of hostages is prohibited. But, I agree, I'm not the expert to be discussing the details of Mr. Karadzic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to move away from questions of theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I just wanted to know, Major, when it was that you made these requests that you wanted to have met. You refer to International Law. Were you meaning international law that protected hostages or prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: What we were requesting was the minimum that we, as a group, thought we were entitled to if the Bosnian Serbs had designated us as prisoners of war, from our understanding of the rights of prisoners of war under the Geneva Convention, because we weren't even getting any of that. We thought that we would start that as a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you did ask for the Red Cross to visit you, as well as a doctor, and to have the right to watch television, and you got all three, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Towards the end, yes. We made these requests early on, and I would have to check the debriefing that you pulled up earlier, but it was -- this letter was drafted, I think, on the fourth or fifth day, something like that. The Red Cross visit I don't think happened until the 11th day, something like that. The doctors -- sorry, the 11th of June. The doctor's visit, I recall, was not until the 8th of June, and it was only after constantly requesting it that this was finally given to us, and only after the Serb side had started to release some of the UN hostages, not beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, and fully understanding how much time has elapsed and the things that can happen to your memory, in response to question 20, you say: [In English] "During the ICRC visit on 8th of June, 1995 ..." [Interpretation] So it was on the 8th of June that the Red Cross visited you. Let us now have a look at the 6th of June. A universities professor visited you, Dr. Sosic, and this is what he says on the front page, the interpreters can help us as well: "Report of a doctor of the military hospital on the visit of POWs, officers of the UN." When it says "zarobljenik" [phoen] in our part of the world, it would be superfluous to say the whole thing, "prisoners of war." It goes without saying that it's a prisoner of war, a "zarobljenik." However, it has been mistranslated here. It should not only say "prisoners," because when you use the verb "zarobiti" [phoen], that means to take an enemy prisoner or an opponent prisoner. So does it show that the professor considered you to be a POW?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I don't know what report this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can help you on this regard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this report. I've not seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, we do see that on the 6th, Dr. Sosic visited you. You made your request on the 4th. On the 6th, you were visited by Dr. Sosic, and on the 8th by the Red Cross. Now, this is Professor Sosic describing the situation that you were in, your physical and mental condition, of all the captives, actually.
