So he visited you on the 5th of June, and on the 6th, he wrote his report. So can we have the next page, please. Professor M. Sosic, Mirko Sosic, who is a senior consult -- who is a professor, and also there is a senior consultant, Dr. Babic. These are top-notch experts who visited you immediately after you had requested that, and they wrote up their report on the 6th of June. Is it true that this is the report on that visit, and you actually said some of the things that are contained in this report; that one was supposed to be released immediately, and that certain measures were proposed, like more fruit and vegetables, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I debated whether to get up, Your Honour, but I think if I don't address these things as they happen, they will continue to intrude. There's more commentary by Dr. Karadzic that is identifying who the experts are when it's not in the record. If it's important to him, he can ask the question or elicit evidence about it. If it is not, in and of itself, an important matter, I don't particularly question the qualifications of these experts, but this is the kind of intrusion of testimony and commentary that we need to discourage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with your observation, Mr. Tieger. You have another lesson today, Mr. Karadzic. Please bear that in mind. So what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My thanks to Mr. Tieger for educating me, for lecturing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, do you agree that Dr. Sosic, a university professor, and Dr. Babic, a senior consultant, visited you, and that this report is based on that visit paid to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Two individuals who are doctors by that name visited us on the 5th of June, yes. And I'm not sure if that report is specific to us or other UNMOs, but you can see that what he requests be provided us, that matches fairly closely with what we had requested of Major Batinic, formerly -- earlier into our detention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D989, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, I believe -- or, actually, I'm asking you to confirm or deny that you saw POWs during your service in various situations, in various theaters of war.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Actually, no, I have not, not as defined by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to ask you something. I believe that you were at different theaters of war on behalf of the UN. Did you ever see POWs who were entitled to satellite telephones and other wireless communications? Does any international law envisage that kind of thing, that they are entitled to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this pertains to what the distinguished Mr. Tieger asked about, taking away communications equipment. When they were taken prisoner, they were forbidden communication. I don't even have a mobile telephone over here right now, so POWs are not entitled to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that that has been asked and answered. I take it you are coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're working until 2.30, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at pages 4 and 5 of 65 ter 19300, 19300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's your debriefing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, pages 4 and 5 of the debriefing, the debriefing entry for June the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, on the 1st of June, you wrote a letter, and you referred to these rights that you had as POWs on the basis of the Geneva Convention: [In English] "... UNMOs discussed the implications of prisoners all under the Geneva Convention. A six-point letter was formulated to Major Batinic with various requests." [Interpretation] Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should be e-court page 11, on the bottom, and then continuing on to page 12.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the 1st of June: [In English] "The UNMO discussed how to deal with captain. Consensus, was that they elected official team representative (other than Rechner and Zidlik, the Serbs speaking UNMOs, so that always two UNMOs could confront the captain, one acting as interpreter). They also felt that they should not deal with captain, but with his superior. They discussed implications of prisoners of war --" [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please: [In English] "... prisoners of war and Geneva Convention." [Interpretation] So here are your requests: [In English] "The request was to Major Batinic, requesting: Contact with next of kin; contact with ICRC; Rechner to be allowed to speak with Professor Koljevic; for members of all three teams to visit their accommodations to pick up clothes; access to news; medical examination of UNMOs."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Captain Vojvodic took some of you to get your clothing from where you had been staying?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, he did that for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So all of these six points were met, more or less?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: By were the 15th of June -- by the end of the 15th of June, yes, which was the 21st day of our captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we have to go back to this. You wrote it up on the 1st, and on the 4th you came in touch with - what's his name? - Batinic, and you handed that over. I don't know when you handed it over. And then on the 5th, you visited by a doctor. On the 8th of June, you were visited by the Red Cross; right? So it was considerably before your period of captivity that these requests were met; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: These requests were made, starting the first day, verbally. When we saw we were not getting a reaction - especially what concerned us most was the phone calls to our next of kin - we then decided to try to do a more formal approach to Major Batinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You wrote that on the 4th of June; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I'd have to go back. Can you scroll back to the previous page? The 1st of June, as you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 1st of June, you discussed it, but earlier on you said that you had handed it over in writing on the 4th of June. Did you manage to speak to your families on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Sorry, there was two questions there, one about handing over the letter and something -- and speaking to our families by telephone. So let me answer the first one. We -- as soon as we drafted the letter, we gave it to Captain Vojvodic. When Major Batinic actually had received it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of you or all of you speak to your families by phone?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: As far as I know, all of us had at least one opportunity to make a supervised two-minute telephone call. So one single two-minute telephone call by the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have the same document, the entry -- just a moment, please. I'm sorry. Page 5. It has to do with the 1st of June yet again. Can we have the next page. I have to find it now, where it says: [In English] "The UNMOs agreed among themselves to give only ID numbers, name, rank, and nationality because of the prisoner of war status given them by the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in the middle, 1930.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Major, the Serbs gave you that status, and you decided to say only what you had to in accordance with the provisions regulating POWs, as stated here; name, rank, and nationality?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't draft this. This was based on discussions with someone, and they drafted it. By "status," that's probably not the best way of phrasing it. What it should say is that the Serbs said, You are POWs, period. That's all we ever got. We never got some sort of document, or list of rights, or even how we were to be treated; nothing. It was just simply that we were told that we are prisoners of war of the Bosnian Serb Army, period. That's all that was ever told to us. And then Major -- or Mr. Bulajic said that he considered us to be combatants. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In one way or another, that is reflected in the parenthesis, which says "given them by the Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that two out of the three pilots from that team were questioned about the possibility of carrying out activities related to forward air controllers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I don't really know what was discussed. This is -- I mean, afterwards they mentioned a little bit about the discussion and that the Bosnian Serb officers were interested in NATO targeting capabilities and that sort of stuff, but I don't know more than what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you kindly to look at the same paragraph: [In English] "The officers departed and then returned after the superiors said they wanted to speak with Zidlik (Czech) and Evans (Ghanaian) who were pilot background. Both the UNMOs were taken to a separate area for questioning. These officers offered to allow Evans to make a call home if he co-operated with them. He declined. They wanted to know how the targets were selected. They also showed Zidlik a bomb fragment which supposedly had grid co-ordinates marked on it and tried to implicate UNMOs as providing these references to NATO." [Interpretation] There is no need for me to read all of this out, there is no need for me to read all of this out. Do you see that the Army of Republika Srpska wondered how it was possible for them to have this kind of information and to target with such precision, and that it was the air force people among the UNMOs that were actually doing that? Do you see that that is what is written here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Again, I don't quite understand. Perhaps there's a problem with the translation, but I'm not sure what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you did mention during the examination-in-chief that you had been accused of acting as forward air controllers; not you, personally, but UNMOs, in general, were accused of co-operating with NATO, in terms of acting as forward air controllers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Actually, my understanding was that I was accused, personally, together with Ole Zidlik and Pavel Teterevsky, of acting as forward air controllers on that news report on that first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But only these two air force men were questioned. You weren't. And who else was there? Who else was there from the air force?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Well, it's stated "Evans." That's Griffiths Evans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the questioning was carried out by a major from the Security Service and that Mladic, General Mladic, was not present at the time, he was not in barracks?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing General Mladic there during my captivity. That's all I can say. Whether he was there or not, I can't say one way or the other. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D306. It's an exhibit, D306. I would like to show you the statement of one of the observers who was held prisoner, Gunnar Westlund from Sweden, so could we please have a look at this document. Just a moment to see what page. Gunnar Westlund, I think that's the right one. Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think if we had page 3 on e-court, that was what we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. The pages in e-court and the pages in the actual document do not always coincide. Para 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In 1995 -- in April 1995, I looked out of our window and I saw a UN vehicle with apparent UNMOs inside it ..." Et cetera, et cetera. "... about 200 metres from our building." May I ask you and all the other parties to read this paragraph. Were you aware of such incidents, Major?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was just to enhance our understanding. What was the Serb side supposed to think of these ghost teams misusing your uniforms and your vehicles and your insignia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness answered that he didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, Major, of any Canadian soldiers who served in Bosnia and Herzegovina as forward air controllers or scouts in the service of NATO?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I had heard that our battalion in Visoko had one -- perhaps two such officers who were trained to be forward air controllers in case they would require support from the air to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the case against the said Nicholas Ribic in Canada, you were a witness, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 65 ter -- 1D2904. Let's first see the first page to identify the document: "In the Federal Court of Canada, Trial Division." Now, could we see in e-court page 138. In the document, it's page 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, may I ask you to look at this passage referring to forward air controllers and the statement of Witness B in this case. He testified that one of forward air controllers was involved in guiding bombs that were dropped on Pale in May 1995. Yes, that's the right page, 138. He was also a major; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know who you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. At first, of course -- well, we better get much more clarity, but this question lacks foundation, given the fact that all we know is that this appears to be somebody who testified in the same case that this witness testified in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic, so that the witness can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You testified in this same case, and you confirm today that guiding did take place, that one of the soldiers in the UN troops was a forward air controller and served in Visoko. Do you know that this person, called Witness B in this case, also confirmed that a forward air controller guided bombs in May 1995 in the area of Pale?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, and again I'm sorry, I really hate to rise this much, but I think that assumes facts not in evidence. I believe the witness, with respect to forward air controllers, spoke about capacity, but not the act of guiding. And it shouldn't be built into questions in this manner if it's not reflected in the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard that, whether you can answer the question whether you knew that this person, Witness B, confirmed that a forward air controller guided bombs in May 1995 in the area of Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know anything more about this person, other than there was someone named Witness B in the proceedings. I was not there for the testimony or to know what he did. The other thing is what I mentioned regarding our battalion in Visoko. I heard that they were supposed to have, in their structure, one -- somebody trained as a forward air controller, if required. If they actually had one there with that battalion at that time, especially at that particular time in May, I don't know. I don't have any of that information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, this is very important. A captain in your national army, serving the United Nations, spends a whole week in Pale, from which you report on anything of consequence. He planned the operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, he says he knows nothing about it. Call Witness B, then, if necessary, if it has any relevance at all. Just put your case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I can just intervene for a moment. We do hope to call Witness B. We're engaged in discussions with the Canadian Government about that. But I think that Dr. Karadzic, although he is not quite doing it exactly the way a lawyer might do it, is trying to put to this witness, to test this witness's credibility, sufficient details about what Witness B has said so that later on you can make an evaluation of this witness's credibility, considering these events took place in the very town that he is located in. So that's the object of what Dr. Karadzic is trying to do, and I think it's a legitimate one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Robinson, the witness has already said that he doesn't know anything more about this person, other than there was someone named Witness B in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I think the object of the questions is to ask the witness whether he was aware of any individuals in the Canadian Armed Forces who were, number 1, conducting surveillance of the target in Pale that was bombed, that had spent a week in the area of Pale prior to -- selecting targets for NATO, that was providing intelligence information as to what was in the very ammunition dump that he was held at, and that later on he goes on to say that there were four to five air controllers in the Pale area. So it seems like all of these items, which are part of our case, ought, in fairness to the witness, to be put to him so that he can comment. And, if, in fact, he has no knowledge of any of those things, then that's fine, but I think we have a right to put that to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I mean, specific discreet questions can, of course, be put to the witness, but it's wrong, in principle, to put to the witness the testimony of another witness when he wasn't -- particularly when he wasn't there at the time that the witness was giving evidence. So you began your intervention quite rightly, Mr. Robinson, by saying Dr. Karadzic wasn't doing it in the way that a lawyer would do it, and that's right. He isn't. What he needs to do is to formulate specific questions to which he can get discreet answers, without reference to a third party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would expect your role in formulating questions on the part of the Defence, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Karadzic, having heard these, put your case to the witness and let's move on, or put your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting. I'm just waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, the gist of my question is this: You are in Pale, and you are reporting from Pale on everything and anything of consequence. How is it possible you were unaware that a member of your army spent a week in Pale and planned NATO attacks on our targets? That's my question. And Mr. Robinson feels what I'm trying to ask, perhaps a little clumsily. But how is it possible you were not aware your captain was in Pale, planning an attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have an elephant under my robes. How is Dr. Karadzic not aware of that? The problem here is obvious. He's assuming facts not in evidence, presenting it to the witness, and we have to rely on the witness to untangle the problems with such approaches. If he wants to put his case to the witness, he can. But he can't assume, in the course of that, that it's been established that there was a member of "your army," as he put it, who spent a week in Pale and planned NATO attacks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. The question is whether -- how is it possible that the witness was not aware, while his army spent a week in Pale. Yes, that's a very compound question. The witness has answered the second part, whether he knew or not -- or whether or not that a member of the UNPROFOR or UNMO spent a week in Pale. Just put simpler questions, if you would like to. Let me put it on your behalf, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Rechner, did you know at the time that an air-strike controller - I'm sorry about the terminology - spent a week in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I don't even recall seeing another Canadian there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The same witness stated that UN observers provided intelligence to NATO. What do you have to say to that? I could show a page from this testimony, and the same witness says that he received from you, from UNMOs, intelligence as to what was contained in our ammunition depots. Were you aware of that, and do you know who provided that intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anyone in my team providing intelligence to NATO, and nor anybody in the UN Military Observer organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 149 of this transcript, the same witness says that there were four teams of forward air controllers in Pale, with four to five men each. Did you observe that massive presence of forward air controllers, and did you report on it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Absolutely not did I observe any such presence in Pale. Therefore, of course, there was no reporting. As I mentioned, I'm not -- I didn't see any of these either Canadian or other air controllers in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were among the last to be released; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you understand this fact, that you were kept almost until the end? In other words, were you aware that the Serb side was waiting with your release until they got back their own four soldiers who had been captured?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I was not aware. In the meeting I had with President Koljevic on the 15th, he said he was hoping that I would have been released earlier, but that there was some technical problems. And that's all he said. What those technical problems were supposed to mean, either transportation, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this case against Ribic, you testified to this circumstance. That's on pages 181 and 182. That was reported on the local news; that is to say, that these four Serbs were held prisoner. Were you -- is it correct, in fact, that these four Serbs were taken prisoner on Vrbanja Bridge?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I had heard on the -- actually, I think it was on my shortwave radio that a French position on the Vrbanja Bridge had been attacked by Serbs, wearing French uniforms with UN blue helmets, and that a battle had ensued, and that the French had captured four of these Serbs. That's all I know. How it was linked -- if it was linked to our release, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You think that Serbs wore French uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That's the way it was reported.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard evidence and seen statements here to the effect that Muslims put on French uniforms and that was the reason why the Serbs and Muslims clashed on Vrbanja Bridge. Let's see 65 ter 13544. 13544.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is an associated exhibit, the OTP notification, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps the Prosecution has the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here that the president of the republic ordered that UNPROFOR members located -- no, that's not it. It should be an order to release UNMOs; 17 June. Yes, this is 17 June. You see here an order was given to free detained -- it's point 11 below: "The Command of the SRK shall, by 1400 hours," on such and such a date, "hand over to the authorities of the MUP of Republika Srpska 26 members of the UN who are being released. The release and hand-over of the detained members shall take place only after the UNPROFOR brings to the Garrison Lukavica four captured members of the VRS." Do you see that it's an all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: What I see on the text is that General Mladic is instructing some of his commanders not to release us, the 26 UN members, until after the 4 VRS members or Bosnian Serb Army soldiers or members are released to Lukavica Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the language is different, that they will be released once the others are released. It does not say they will not be released. There is a slight difference. One group will be released as soon as the other group is released. Does this look like an exchange to you, Major?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: I think there's a problem. If you say -- your version does not match the English translation here. The English translation, you can see it's the "26 UN members will only be released (only be done after UNPROFOR brings four captured VRS members to the Lukavica Garrison." So the four Serbs have to be released first before we can be released, is the way I understand that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. Do you need more to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think, Your Excellency, that we have gone through most of it. I have a few questions left, but basically we can conclude soon. Are we supposed to conclude now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you conclude in five minutes' time? Do you have re-examination, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can curtail it, in the interests, Your Honour, but there is one matter I'd like to address. I will simply see if I can -- I'll do it as efficiently as possible or perhaps just be permitted to point the Court to documents that may cover the issue as well. So I'll be as quick as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Try to conclude in three minutes, Mr. Karadzic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, you wrote a letter to Captain Vojvodic; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No, I don't recall writing a letter to Captain Vojvodic. It was to Colonel Djurdjic and Major Batinic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djurdjic, sorry. Let me just try to find this letter. Is it turned on -- sorry, is it exhibited as part of an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously it hasn't even been up-loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that letter to Captain Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that was -- I mean, not the detail in my memory now, but it was written on the evening of the 29th of May, at the request of Captain Vojvodic, concerning the meeting with Professor Koljevic, and he said he wanted -- or Colonel Djurdjic wanted to know the details of what I wanted to discuss with Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This previous document is already part of an exhibit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you write to anyone after your release?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Write about what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you write to any Serb officer after your release?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then one of your men must have written, expressing gratitude for the treatment, et cetera. But since it was not you, we won't look at it. Thank you, Major. I'm sorry you went through what you went through, but I cannot help also thinking of the Serbs who were there at the time suffering from NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be very quick and expedite it by referring to a document Mr. Karadzic referred to repeatedly himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Major, you were asked questions by the accused about the man who lost his sheep and who, according to Mr. Karadzic, also lost a family member. I believe at the earlier portion of your transcript, you had referred to the fact that the man said something about a missing relative. Is it correct, as reflected in P22011, that is, the document to which Dr. Karadzic referred you, the debriefing to which he referred to you repeatedly, that you encountered that person again and learned that, in fact, his missing relative was someone who had gone out for a walk and returned shortly afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. This person who attacked me later explained that his missing relative had simply gone out for a walk and returned safe and sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I shouldn't call that P. I should call it 65 ter 22011. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, Dr. Karadzic made repeated references to phone calls. Again, turning to 65 ter 22011, to which Dr. Karadzic referred repeatedly, at page R103-8644, which was read out by Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Evans is offered a phone call if he'll co-operate, and he declined. And at the previous page, you are told, on the 30th of May, that if you provide notes about other UNMOs, then they could arrange for you to make a phone call home. Is it correct that the prospect of granting you phone calls to your family was used as leverage in an effort to get the UNMOs to do something that their captors wanted?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK RECHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that was certainly our understanding, that they were using the bait of our need to contact our next of kin by telephones to force us to do things against our will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two clarifications, briefly, please, lest the Chamber be misled. Just two brief qualifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Karadzic? What is it related to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, Major, did you make telephone calls, nevertheless, without having these additional requests met? When you invoked the status of POW, were you allowed to make telephone calls without having to do anything in return? Secondly, at the point in time when that man was angry, when he realised that his relative was still alive, was he still angry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think we need the assistance of the witness in that regard, and the clarification won't be necessary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise, Your Honour. There's one matter that needs clarification. I can try and do it through the tapes or try to do it directly with the witness, and I apologise for raising that late. It was in the earlier testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that concludes your evidence, Mr. Rechner, Major Rechner. On behalf of the Bench and the Tribunal, as a whole, thank you very much for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one quick matter before we rise. We are seized of the motion from the Defence to suspend the proceedings for three months, starting as of 15th of February, so we would appreciate it if we could have your response as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour, understood. Could I clarify for the record, very quickly, I referred, during that very quick redirect, to 65 ter 22011. It should be 19300. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Could do that -- file it before Wednesday of next week, 9th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no reason at this point to think otherwise, but if we think that's some form of problem, we'll let the Court know as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll rise, and we'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.45 p.m.,
